:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a Challenging System of Linear Equations Using Substitution

17592186073923.:activity/title: Solving Systems of Equations by Substitution

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose that we want to solve, *without* using graphs, the following system of linear equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+y &=4 \\ x-2 &=y\,\end{aligned}\right.
$$

In order to solve the system without a graph, we will need to combine the equations into a single equation that can be solved using algebraic manipulation.

One way to combine the equations is called the **substitution method.** To use the substitution method, we substitute for one variable in terms of the other.

For instance, notice that we can make $y$ the subject of the second equation:

$$
\color{red}y=x - 2
$$

Substituting this expression for $y$ into the first equation, we get an equation that we can solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}x+y & =4 \\ x+(x-2) & =4 \\ 2x-2 & =4 \\ 2x & =6 \\ x & =3\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $x=3.$ But we also need to figure out what $y$ is. We can do this by substituting $x=3$ back into the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =x-2 \\ y & =3-2 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 3$ and $y = 1$, which can be written as $\left(3, 1\right).$

**Note:** Whenever we isolate the variable in one equation, we have to substitute it into the *other* equation. We cannot substitute a variable into the same equation it came from, because this will not give us any more information about the variable.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Solve the following system of equations:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-y &=4 \\ x+2y &=16\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It doesn't matter which equation we pick first, so we choose the easiest one. In this case, the first equation looks like the easiest.

Using the first equation, we can isolate $x$ by adding $y$ to both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x-y & =4 \\ x & =4+y\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we replace $x$ with $4+y$ in the second equation and solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	x+2y &=16 \
	(4+y) + 2y &=16\
	4+3y &=16\
	3y &=12\
	y &=4
}
$$

If we now substitute $y=4$ into $x=4+y$, then we can find the value of $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	x &= 4 + y \
	   &= 4 + (4) \
	   &=8
}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x = 8$ and $y = 4$, which can be written as $(8, 4).$

Sometimes, it's handy to assign a number to each equation in a system, so that we can refer to them more easily:
![](images/77/77459b19bb1fd1f28e05e6f613e4e49af34595eae33eeeca584d65a289f7ea2c.svg)

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $\color{blue}(2)$, we can solve for $u$ as follows:

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+6v-8 &= 0 \
2u+6v &= 8 \

u &= \dfrac{8-6v}{2} \
u &= 4 - 3v
}
$$

Then, we substitute $u=4-3v$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$ and solve for $v\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \
	2(4-3v)+9v-6 &= 0 \
	8-6v+9v-6 &= 0 \
2+3v &= 0 \
3v &= -2 \
v &= -\dfrac{2}{3}
}
$$

If we now substitute $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$ into equation $\color{red}(1)$, then we can find the value of $u\mathbin{:}$

$$
\eqalign{
	2u+9v-6 &= 0 \
	2u+9\left(-\dfrac{2}{3}\right) -6 &= 0 \
	2u-6-6 &= 0 \
	2u-12 &= 0 \
	2u &= 12 \
	u &= 6
}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $u=6$ and $v=-\dfrac{2}{3}$, which can be written as $\left(6,-\dfrac{2}{3}\right).$

\begin{aligned}p+2q & =9 \\ (5)+2q & =9 \\ 2q & =4 \\ q & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $p=5,\,q=2.$ So,

$$
p-q=5-2=3.
$$

:step/content.:question/problem:
Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a+b?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2b=6a+14 \\ 5b+25=0\end{aligned}
$$
:step/content.:question/worked-solution:
We number the equations so that we can refer to them more easily:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2b=6a+14 & \,\,(1) \\ 5b+25=0. & \,\,(2)\end{aligned}
$$

We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. Using equation $(2),$ we can solve for $b$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}5b+25 & =0 \\ 5b & =-25 \\ b & =-5\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute $b=-5$ into equation $(1)$ and solve for $a:$

$$
\begin{aligned}2(-5) & =6a+14 \\ -10 & =6a+14 \\ -10-14 & =6a \\ 6a & =-24 \\ a & =-4\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=-4,\,b=-5.$ So,

$$
a+b=-4+(-5)=-4-5=-9.
$$

:step/content.:question/problem:
Given the system of equations below, what is the value of $a-b?$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}a=7 \\ 3a+6b=15\end{aligned}
$$
:step/content.:question/worked-solution:
We will isolate a variable in one of the equations and then substitute it into the other equation. It so happens that the first equation is already solved for $a:$

$$
a=7
$$

If we now substitute $a=7$ into $3a+6b=15,$ then we can find the value of $b:$

$$
\begin{aligned}3a+6b & =15 \\ 3(7)+6b & =15 \\ 6b & =-6 \\ b & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $a=7,\,b=-1.$ So,

$$
a-b=7-(-1)=7+1=8.
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Let's consider a system of linear equations where the corresponding coefficient matrix is singular. For example, consider the following system and its associated augmented matrix:
![](images/6a/6a69daf7712312876b0ec97c540bbc472e46a7938beb8a59e694a04ad0b1d8c6.svg)

To solve the system, we can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as usual. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -5 \\ -3 & 6 & 15\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now
![](images/a8/a8bfe3f6b27247ee9b27db8346fd94fb9068c85dec6f4a71517a821dee48dbf3.svg)

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x - 2y = -5.
$$

Finally, we describe the **general solution** of our system.

- The first variable in our equation, $x,$ is called a **basic variable**.

- The second variable in our equation, $y,$ is called a **free variable**.

Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x = -5+2y.$ So the general solution of the system is
![](images/0b/0ba4a232f29dd6fce2a8f6d7cda39b4f5b192c20fc91fe4403dfe648231382c5.svg)
where the free variable $y$ is any number.

In vector form, this solution is written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5+2y \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+y[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is the equation of a straight line on a plane. Any point on this line satisfies our system of equations.

If we want to find some **particular solution** of the system, we simply choose some particular value of $y$ and find the corresponding value of $x$ on the line. For example, if we choose $y=0,$ then the corresponding value is $x=-5$ and the particular solution is $x=-5,$ $y=0.$

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 & 0 \\ 2 & -10 & 3\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\{\begin{aligned}x-5y=0 \\ 0x+0y=3.\end{aligned}
$$

However, the final equation $0x+0y=3$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=3,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a Singular 2x2 System of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Given a $2 \times 2$ system of linear equations, we have the following possibilities for the number of solutions:

- The system has exactly *one solution* if and only if the respective coefficient matrix is non-singular (meaning that the determinant is not zero). Such systems are called **consistent independent**.

- The system has *infinitely many solutions* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s. These systems are called **consistent dependent**.

- The system has *no solution* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s on the left-hand side and a non-zero element on the right-hand side. These are called **inconsistent** systems.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

**Note:** A system of linear equations of the form 
![](images/cb/cb397dd01794f28ff11c01079e287d63175e439c8bbaa85cd02dc61689780fa8.svg)
where we have only $0$'s on the right-hand side, is called **homogeneous**. A homogeneous system always has at least one solution, namely, the solution $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle 0,0 \rangle.$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: The Number of Solutions of a 2x2 System

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Sometimes, a system of equations might not have any solutions. For example, consider the following augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is
![](images/e8/e8c64d8be247afd3e8ab02abc69e33635ef0234dbcbbc60f42379021a39a58a2.svg)

The final equation, $0x+0y=10,$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=10,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the augmented matrix $M$ given by 
![](images/97/9773630254747a4bbd072bd44a6263bdd078fa09005b1bb5f51c48b894d67daf.svg)

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce $M$ to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system represented by the matrix.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Reducing $M$ to echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -12 & 4\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-4){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -3 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

![](images/43/43b9b089e0f93e63acf386bb605a0e3751cc8660899ce19d23835f9f79918bcc.svg)

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x - 3y = 1.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=1+3y,$ and the general solution is

![](images/4a/4a598a80f2f14715d1f10d182b3f80887c7586beabecc2a329119b624c19a4fa.svg)

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1+3y \\ y\end{bmatrix}=⟨1+3y,\,y⟩,\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

However, the final equation $0x+0y=-3$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=-3,$ which is a false statement.

17592186048853.:topic/title: Solving 2x2 Singular Systems of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Let's consider a system of linear equations where the corresponding coefficient matrix is singular. For example, consider the following system and its associated augmented matrix:
![](images/6a/6a69daf7712312876b0ec97c540bbc472e46a7938beb8a59e694a04ad0b1d8c6.svg)

To solve the system, we can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as usual. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -5 \\ -3 & 6 & 15\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now
![](images/a8/a8bfe3f6b27247ee9b27db8346fd94fb9068c85dec6f4a71517a821dee48dbf3.svg)

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x - 2y = -5.
$$

Finally, we describe the **general solution** of our system.

- The first variable in our equation, $x,$ is called a **basic variable**.

- The second variable in our equation, $y,$ is called a **free variable**.

Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x = -5+2y.$ So the general solution of the system is
![](images/0b/0ba4a232f29dd6fce2a8f6d7cda39b4f5b192c20fc91fe4403dfe648231382c5.svg)
where the free variable $y$ is any number.

In vector form, this solution is written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5+2y \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+y[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is the equation of a straight line on a plane. Any point on this line satisfies our system of equations.

If we want to find some **particular solution** of the system, we simply choose some particular value of $y$ and find the corresponding value of $x$ on the line. For example, if we choose $y=0,$ then the corresponding value is $x=-5$ and the particular solution is $x=-5,$ $y=0.$

Consider the system of linear equations

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-6y &=2 \\ -4x+24y &=-10.\end{aligned}\right.

Use the standard method of Gaussian elimination to reduce the augmented matrix $M$ of the system to row echelon form, and then find the general solution of the linear system.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -6 & 2 \\ -4 & 24 & -10\end{bmatrix}
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -6 & 2 \\ -4 & 24 & -10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+4{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -6 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-6y &=2 \\ 0x+0y &=-2.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

However, the final equation $0x+0y=-2$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=-2,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Solving a Singular 2x2 System of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Given a $2 \times 2$ system of linear equations, we have the following possibilities for the number of solutions:

- The system has exactly *one solution* if and only if the respective coefficient matrix is non-singular (meaning that the determinant is not zero). Such systems are called **consistent independent**.

- The system has *infinitely many solutions* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s. These systems are called **consistent dependent**.

- The system has *no solution* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s on the left-hand side and a non-zero element on the right-hand side. These are called **inconsistent** systems.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

**Note:** A system of linear equations of the form 
![](images/cb/cb397dd01794f28ff11c01079e287d63175e439c8bbaa85cd02dc61689780fa8.svg)
where we have only $0$'s on the right-hand side, is called **homogeneous**. A homogeneous system always has at least one solution, namely, the solution $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle 0,0 \rangle.$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: The Number of Solutions of a 2x2 System

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Sometimes, a system of equations might not have any solutions. For example, consider the following augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}M=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 & 10\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is
![](images/e8/e8c64d8be247afd3e8ab02abc69e33635ef0234dbcbbc60f42379021a39a58a2.svg)

The final equation, $0x+0y=10,$ has no solution. It simplifies to $0=10,$ which is a false statement.

So, there is no pair $x,y$ that satisfies both equations in the system. Consequently, the overall system has no solution.

17592186106000.:activity/title: Solving 2x2 Singular Systems of Equations Using Gaussian Elimination

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Let's consider a system of linear equations where the corresponding coefficient matrix is singular. For example, consider the following system and its associated augmented matrix:
![](images/6a/6a69daf7712312876b0ec97c540bbc472e46a7938beb8a59e694a04ad0b1d8c6.svg)

To solve the system, we can reduce $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as usual. We have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -5 \\ -3 & 6 & 15\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 & -5 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now
![](images/a8/a8bfe3f6b27247ee9b27db8346fd94fb9068c85dec6f4a71517a821dee48dbf3.svg)

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y = 0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x - 2y = -5.
$$

Finally, we describe the **general solution** of our system.

- The first variable in our equation, $x,$ is called a **basic variable**.

- The second variable in our equation, $y,$ is called a **free variable**.

Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x = -5+2y.$ So the general solution of the system is
![](images/0b/0ba4a232f29dd6fce2a8f6d7cda39b4f5b192c20fc91fe4403dfe648231382c5.svg)
where the free variable $y$ is any number.

In vector form, this solution is written as

$$
\begin{aligned}[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5+2y \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-5 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+y[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that this is the equation of a straight line on a plane. Any point on this line satisfies our system of equations.

If we want to find some **particular solution** of the system, we simply choose some particular value of $y$ and find the corresponding value of $x$ on the line. For example, if we choose $y=0,$ then the corresponding value is $x=-5$ and the particular solution is $x=-5,$ $y=0.$

17592186266013.:question/worked-solution:
First, we set up the augmented matrix for the system:

$$
M=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 8 & 4 \\ -3 & 10 & 6\end{bmatrix}
$$

Reducing $M$ to row echelon form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 8 & 4 \\ -3 & 12 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{1} & :=-\frac{1}{2}{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 & -2 \\ -3 & 12 & 6\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

The corresponding system is now

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-4y &=-2 \\ 0x+0y &=0.\end{aligned}\right.
$$

Since any pair of numbers $x,y$ is a solution of the final equation $0x+0y=0,$ we can remove this equation from the system. So, our system now consists of a single equation

$$
x-4y=-2.
$$

The first variable $(x)$ is the basic variable, and the second variable $(y)$ is the free variable. Solving for the basic variable $(x)$ in terms of the free variable $(y),$ we get $x=4y-2,$ and the general solution is

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x &=4y-2 \\ y &=y\end{aligned}\right.
$$

where $y$ is an arbitrary number. 

In vector form, the general solution can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4y-2 \\ y\end{bmatrix},\,y\in (-\infty ,\infty ).\end{aligned}
$$

Given a $2 \times 2$ system of linear equations, we have the following possibilities for the number of solutions:

- The system has exactly *one solution* if and only if the respective coefficient matrix is non-singular (meaning that the determinant is not zero). Such systems are called **consistent independent**.

- The system has *infinitely many solutions* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s. These systems are called **consistent dependent**.

- The system has *no solution* if the second row in the standard echelon form contains only $0$'s on the left-hand side and a non-zero element on the right-hand side. These are called **inconsistent** systems.

![](images/16/1692fbea298339ff839cf2f14986d51af45d1ec72b2b7d0de179336bdef40c0e.png)

**Note:** A system of linear equations of the form 
![](images/cb/cb397dd01794f28ff11c01079e287d63175e439c8bbaa85cd02dc61689780fa8.svg)
where we have only $0$'s on the right-hand side, is called **homogeneous**. A homogeneous system always has at least one solution, namely, the solution $x=0$ and $y=0.$ Or, in vector form, $\langle 0,0 \rangle.$

If we want to add (or subtract) three or more matrices, all operations should be done elementwise. For example, suppose
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Sum or Difference of Three or More Matrices

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Since addition and subtraction of matrices are performed elementwise, they have the same properties as addition and subtraction of real numbers.

For example, if $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are three $m \times n$ matrices then we can add them in any order:

$$
(A+B)+C = A+(B+C) = A+B+C
$$

Moreover, we can distribute a subtraction over matrices in parentheses:

$$
A - (B + C) = A - B - C
$$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: Properties of Matrix Addition and Subtraction

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find $A+C-(B+A)$, if
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ \sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}$
$B=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
$C=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -6 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we simplify the expression by distributing the subtraction over the matrices in the parentheses: 

$$
\begin{aligned}A+C-(B+A) & =A+C-B-A \\  & =\cancel{A}+C-B-\cancel{A} \\  & =C-B\end{aligned}
$$

We are left with a single subtraction. So, we subtract the corresponding entries of the two matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}C-B & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -6 & 1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3-3 & -1-(-1) \\ 1-2 & 2-0 \\ -6-(-4) & 1-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we simplify the expression by distributing the subtraction over the matrices in the parentheses:

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)-C-(B-C) & =A+B-C-B+C \\  & =A+\cancel{B}-\cancel{C}-\cancel{B}+\cancel{C} \\  & =A\end{aligned}
$$

We are left with a single matrix. So, the result is 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & 7 \\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Sum or Difference of Three or More Matrices

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Since addition and subtraction of matrices are performed elementwise, they have the same properties as addition and subtraction of real numbers.

For example, if $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are three $m \times n$ matrices then we can add them in any order:

$$
(A+B)+C = A+(B+C) = A+B+C
$$

Moreover, we can distribute a subtraction over matrices in parentheses:

$$
A - (B + C) = A - B - C
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Find $A+C-(B+A)$, if
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ \sqrt{2} & 0 \\ 0 & -2\end{bmatrix}$
$B=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
$C=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -6 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we simplify the expression by distributing the subtraction over the matrices in the parentheses: 

$$
\begin{aligned}A+C-(B+A) & =A+C-B-A \\  & =\cancel{A}+C-B-\cancel{A} \\  & =C-B\end{aligned}
$$

We are left with a single subtraction. So, we subtract the corresponding entries of the two matrices:

$$
\begin{aligned}C-B & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2 \\ -6 & 1\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 0 \\ -4 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3-3 & -1-(-1) \\ 1-2 & 2-0 \\ -6-(-4) & 1-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

If we want to add (or subtract) three or more matrices, all operations should be done elementwise. For example, suppose
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}$
$B=\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}$
$C=\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5 \\ -2\end{bmatrix}$
Then we can calculate ${A}+{B}-{C}$ by performing the operations on each corresponding entry, as follows: $$ \begin{aligned}A+B-C & =\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 5 \\ -2\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1+(-1)-0 \\ 1+2-5 \\ -1+0-(-2)\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned} $$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We add two matrices by adding the corresponding entries. We can only do this if they have the same number of rows and columns, that is, they have the same dimensions.

For example, consider the matrices

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix},\qquad B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We see that both $A$ and $B$ are $2\times 2$ matrices, so we can add them. The sum ${A} + {B}\,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}A+B & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+1 & 3+0 \\ 2+0 & 4+(-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, the sum of two matrices is another matrix with the same dimensions.

$$
A - (B + C) = A - B - C
$$

$$

In mathematics, rectangular arrays containing numbers are called **matrices**. 

As an example, consider the matrix $A$ below:

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 3 \\ 4 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 6\end{bmatrix}
$$

This particular matrix has $3$ rows and $3$ columns. The numbers in the matrix are called **entries** or **elements.**

The number of rows and columns in a matrix does not need to be the same. For example, consider another matrix that has $3$ rows and $4$ columns:

$$
M = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 13 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 & -5\end{bmatrix}
$$

The **dimensions** of the matrix are the number of rows and the number of columns. For example, the matrix $M$ shown above has $3$ rows and $4$ columns. So, we write the dimensions of $M$ as $3 \times 4$ (read as "three by four").

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Determining the Dimensions of a Matrix with One Row or Column

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Some matrices have only one column, for instance

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 13\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B = \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
C = \begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Here, $A$ is a $2\times 1$ matrix, $B$ is a $4\times 1$ matrix, and $C$ is a $3\times 1$ matrix. These types of matrices are often called **column vectors**.

Other matrices have only one row, for instance

$$
D = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
E = \begin{bmatrix}13 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
F = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Here, $D$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix, $E$ is a $1\times 3$ matrix, and $F$ is a $1\times 4$ matrix. These types of matrices are often called **row vectors**.

**Note:** Every number can be thought of as a $1\times 1$ matrix. For instance, we can consider the number $5$ as the matrix

$$
{G}
=\begin{bmatrix}\,5\,\end{bmatrix}.
$$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: Matrices With One Row or Column

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
A **square matrix** is a matrix where the number of rows is equal to the number of columns. For example, the matrix
$A =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}$
is a square matrix because it has $2$ rows and $2$ columns. Its dimensions are $2 \times 2.$ In general, the dimensions of a square matrix are $n \times n.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:

- The matrix $B$ has $3$ rows and $2$ columns. So, its dimensions are $3 \times 2.$ $\quad{\color{green}\checkmark}$

- The matrix $C$ has $1$ row and $3$ columns. So, its dimensions are $1 \times 3.$ $\quad{\color{red}\times}$

Therefore, only $B$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix.

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying a Matrix by Its Description

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Matrices arise naturally in *many* real-world problems. Weather forecasting, image processing and computer graphics, video games, and online customization algorithms are just a few of the many applications of matrices. Let's consider an example where we can use a matrix to model bus routes in a city. The diagram below shows the bus routes between three stations (Station A, Station B, and Station C) in a particular city, where $A, B,$ and $C$ represent the stations and the arrows represent the directed routes between them. ![](images/cb/cbdf5c2470229ae3ba10ee18bccd2dc764407897397466b157474bf2b819f5d9.png) Note that the circles $A,B,$ and $C$ in our diagram are called **nodes**. We wish to represent this same diagram using a matrix. Let's start by putting this information into a table like the one below:
To From
ABC
A
B
C
Let's now fill in the rows of our table. We begin by considering all of the bus routes from Station A to the other stations: - There are $\color{blue}0$ bus routes from $A$ to itself. - There is $\color{blue}1$ bus route from $A$ to $B.$ - There is $\color{blue}1$ bus route from $A$ to $C.$ Filling in the first row of the table, we get the following:
To From
ABC
A$\color{blue} 0$$\color{blue} 1$$\color{blue} 1$
B
C
Filling in the remaining rows in the same way, we get:
To From
ABC
A$0$$1$$1$
B$0$$1$$2$
C$1$$0$$0$
Finally, keeping only the essential information, we obtain the following matrix: $$ \begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix} $$

So, there is only one route from $A$ to $A,$ and so $a=1.$ - No arrows are starting at Station B and ending at Station B. So, there are no routes from $B$ to $B,$ and so $b=0.$ - There is $1$ arrow starting at Station C and ending at Station A. So, there is only one route from $C$ to $A,$ and so $c=1.$ As a result, our route matrix is the following:

Therefore, $$ a+b+c = 1+0+1 = 2. $$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Matrices for Route Planning

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
In mathematics, rectangular arrays containing numbers are called **matrices**. 

As an example, consider the matrix $A$ below:

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}2 & 1 & 3 \\ 4 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & -4 & 6\end{bmatrix}
$$

This particular matrix has $3$ rows and $3$ columns. The numbers in the matrix are called **entries** or **elements.**

The number of rows and columns in a matrix does not need to be the same. For example, consider another matrix that has $3$ rows and $4$ columns:

$$
M = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 13 & 4 & 2 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 & 0 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 & -5\end{bmatrix}
$$

The **dimensions** of the matrix are the number of rows and the number of columns. For example, the matrix $M$ shown above has $3$ rows and $4$ columns. So, we write the dimensions of $M$ as $3 \times 4$ (read as "three by four").

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Some matrices have only one column, for instance

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 13\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B = \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
C = \begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Here, $A$ is a $2\times 1$ matrix, $B$ is a $4\times 1$ matrix, and $C$ is a $3\times 1$ matrix. These types of matrices are often called **column vectors**.

Other matrices have only one row, for instance

$$
D = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
E = \begin{bmatrix}13 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
F = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Here, $D$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix, $E$ is a $1\times 3$ matrix, and $F$ is a $1\times 4$ matrix. These types of matrices are often called **row vectors**.

**Note:** Every number can be thought of as a $1\times 1$ matrix. For instance, we can consider the number $5$ as the matrix

$$
{G}
=\begin{bmatrix}\,5\,\end{bmatrix}.
$$

17592186088891.:tutorial/content:
Some matrices have only one column, for instance

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ 13\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B = \begin{bmatrix}0 \\ -1 \\ 3 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
C = \begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}
$$

Here, $A$ is a $2\times 1$ matrix, $B$ is a $4\times 1$ matrix, and $C$ is a $3\times 1$ matrix. These types of matrices are often called **column vectors**.

Other matrices have only one row, for instance

$$
D = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
E = \begin{bmatrix}13 & -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
F = \begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 & 3 & 1\end{bmatrix}
$$

Here, $D$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix, $E$ is a $1\times 3$ matrix, and $F$ is a $1\times 4$ matrix. These types of matrices are often called **row vectors**.

**Note:** Every number can be thought of as a $1\times 1$ matrix. For instance, we can consider the number $5$ as the matrix

$$
{G}
=\begin{bmatrix}\,5\,\end{bmatrix}.
$$

17592186088898.:tutorial/content:
A **square matrix** is a matrix where the number of rows is equal to the number of columns. For example, the matrix
$A =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}$
is a square matrix because it has $2$ rows and $2$ columns. Its dimensions are $2 \times 2.$ In general, the dimensions of a square matrix are $n \times n.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
- The matrix $A$ has $2$ rows and $3$ columns. So, its dimensions are $2 \times 3.$ $\quad{\color{red}\times}$

- The matrix $B$ has $3$ rows and $2$ columns. So, its dimensions are $3 \times 2.$ $\quad{\color{green}\checkmark}$

- The matrix $C$ has $1$ row and $3$ columns. So, its dimensions are $1 \times 3.$ $\quad{\color{red}\times}$

Therefore, only $B$ is a $3 \times 2$ matrix.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
When we reduce a matrix to row echelon form, the number of *pivot* columns plus the number of *non-pivot* columns always equals the total number of columns of the matrix. 

By translating this into the language of vector spaces, we get the **rank-nullity theorem**. The rank-nullity theorem relates the rank of a matrix to the dimension of its null space:

*Let $A$ be a matrix (not necessarily square) with $n$ columns. Then,*

$$
\textrm{dim(Col}(A)) + \textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n),
$$

*or, equivalently,*

$$
\textrm{rank}(A) + \textrm{nullity}(A) = n.
$$

For example, suppose that for some matrix $A,$ we have

![](images/30/30f6472f02a4ac47f285fff05e0cdbf56367acdd18231271dc3dccf0040901bd.svg)

We can use the rank-nullity theorem to calculate $\textrm{rank}(A).$

In this case, we must have $n=4,$ since this is the number of components in each of the vectors of the null space. 

Also, we must have $\textrm{nullity}(A)=2,$ since 
![](images/b5/b5f38590a71a2f8e1f29a5ba98920a10037737c1ebcbd3fd60f08a3e47555141.svg)

Therefore, using the rank-nullity theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ \text{rank}(A)+2 & =4 \\ \text{rank}(A) & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

According to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\textrm{rank}(A) + \textrm{nullity}(A) = n.
$$

For the given matrix, we have $n=5,$ and since $\mathcal{B}$ is formed by $3$ vectors, $\textrm{rank}(A) = 3.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ 3+\text{nullity}(A) & =5 \\ \text{nullity}(A) & =5-3 \\ \text{dim(Null}(A)) & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Since $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{5} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=5=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A)=n.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false.  Since $A$ has $2$ pivot columns, we have $\text{rank}(A)=2.$

- Statement II is false. For the matrix $A,$ the number of the columns is $n=5.$ Now, since $\text{rank}(A)\ne 5,$ then by the invertible matrix theorem, we have that $A$ is not invertible.

- Statement III is true. According to  the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ 2+\text{nullity}(A) & =5 \\ \text{nullity}(A) & =5-2 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is " III only."

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Rank or Nullity of a Matrix Using the Rank-Nullity Theorem

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
When we reduce a matrix to row echelon form, the number of *pivot* columns plus the number of *non-pivot* columns always equals the total number of columns of the matrix. 

By translating this into the language of vector spaces, we get the **rank-nullity theorem**. The rank-nullity theorem relates the rank of a matrix to the dimension of its null space:

*Let $A$ be a matrix (not necessarily square) with $n$ columns. Then,*

$$
\textrm{dim(Col}(A)) + \textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n),
$$

*or, equivalently,*

$$
\textrm{rank}(A) + \textrm{nullity}(A) = n.
$$

For example, suppose that for some matrix $A,$ we have

![](images/30/30f6472f02a4ac47f285fff05e0cdbf56367acdd18231271dc3dccf0040901bd.svg)

We can use the rank-nullity theorem to calculate $\textrm{rank}(A).$

In this case, we must have $n=4,$ since this is the number of components in each of the vectors of the null space. 

Also, we must have $\textrm{nullity}(A)=2,$ since 
![](images/b5/b5f38590a71a2f8e1f29a5ba98920a10037737c1ebcbd3fd60f08a3e47555141.svg)

Therefore, using the rank-nullity theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ \text{rank}(A)+2 & =4 \\ \text{rank}(A) & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{4} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=4=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A)=n.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since 

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\{[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ 2{x}_{1} \\ -3{x}_{1} \\ -4{x}_{1}\end{aligned}]\,|\,{x}_{1}\in R\}=\text{Span}\{\,[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ -3 \\ -4\end{aligned}]\}
$$

 
we have that $\text{nullity}(A)=1.$

Now,  for the matrix $A,$ the number of columns is $n=4,$ so according to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ \text{rank}(A)+1 & =4 \\ \text{rank}(A) & =4-1 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. Since $\text{rank}(A)=3\ne 4,$ then, by the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{4}.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $\text{rank}(A)=3\ne 4$, according to the  invertible matrix theorem $A$ can't be an invertible matrix.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
When we reduce a matrix to row echelon form, the number of *pivot* columns plus the number of *non-pivot* columns always equals the total number of columns of the matrix. 

By translating this into the language of vector spaces, we get the **rank-nullity theorem**. The rank-nullity theorem relates the rank of a matrix to the dimension of its null space:

*Let $A$ be a matrix (not necessarily square) with $n$ columns. Then,*

$$
\textrm{dim(Col}(A)) + \textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \textrm{dim}(\mathbb{R}^n),
$$

*or, equivalently,*

$$
\textrm{rank}(A) + \textrm{nullity}(A) = n.
$$

For example, suppose that for some matrix $A,$ we have

![](images/30/30f6472f02a4ac47f285fff05e0cdbf56367acdd18231271dc3dccf0040901bd.svg)

We can use the rank-nullity theorem to calculate $\textrm{rank}(A).$

In this case, we must have $n=4,$ since this is the number of components in each of the vectors of the null space. 

Also, we must have $\textrm{nullity}(A)=2,$ since 
![](images/b5/b5f38590a71a2f8e1f29a5ba98920a10037737c1ebcbd3fd60f08a3e47555141.svg)

Therefore, using the rank-nullity theorem, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ \text{rank}(A)+2 & =4 \\ \text{rank}(A) & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\textrm{Col}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n.

:step/content.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true, given that $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and  $det(A)=1?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A$ is not invertible

- **II.** $\text{rank}(A)=4$

- **III.** $A$ has $5$ pivot columns
:step/content.:question/worked-solution:
Since $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{5} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=5=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. 

- Statement I is false. Indeed,   a matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ Since here we have $det(A)=1\ne 0,$ our matrix $A$ must be  invertible.

- Statement II is false. Indeed, by the invertible matrix theorem
$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\text{rank}(A)=5.$

- Statement III is true. Since $\text{rank}(A)=5$,  it must be $\text{dim(Col}(A))=5$ which, in turn, means that  $A$ has $5$ pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

17592186184755.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true, given that $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and 

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\text{Span}\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\}?
$$

I. The number of non-pivot columns in $A$ is equal to $3$

II. $\text{Col}(A)={R}^{4}$

III. $\text{rank}(A)=2$
17592186184755.:question/worked-solution:
Since $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{4} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=4=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A)=n.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since the generating vectors in 

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\text{Span}\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\}
$$

are linearly independent, we conclude that the number of non-pivot columns in $A$ is equal to $2.$

- Statement II is false. Since $\text{nullity}(A)=2\ne 0,$ then by the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{4}.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for the matrix $A,$ the number of columns is $n=4.$ Now, according to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ \text{rank}(A)+2 & =4 \\ \text{rank}(A) & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

II. $A$ is invertible

III. $\text{nullity}(A)=1$
17592186184757.:question/worked-solution:
Since $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{4} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=4=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A)=n.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, since $A$ has $3$ pivot columns, we have $\text{rank}(A)=3.$

- Statement II is false. For the matrix $A,$ the number of the columns is $n=4.$ Now, since $\text{rank}(A)\ne 4,$ then by the invertible matrix theorem, we have that $A$ is not invertible.

- Statement III is true. According to  the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

 Thus,  according to the invertible matrix theorem $A$ is  **not** an invertible matrix.

$$

$$

Since $A$ is a $6\times 6$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{6} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=6=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A)=n.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since $A$ has $n=6$ columns and $2$ of them are non-pivot ones, it follows that    

$$
\text{dim(Col}(A))=6-2=4\ne 6.
$$

 Thus, according to the invertible matrix theorem $A$ can't be an invertible matrix.

- Statement II is false. Since $\text{dim(Col}(A))=4$,  then $\text{rank}(A)=4.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, since $n=6$, according to  the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ 4+\text{nullity}(A) & =6 \\ \text{nullity}(A) & =6-4 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:step/content.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true, given that $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix and 

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\text{Span}\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\}?
$$

I. The number of non-pivot columns in $A$ is equal to $3$

II. $\text{Col}(A)={R}^{4}$

III. $\text{rank}(A)=2$
:step/content.:question/worked-solution:
Since $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{4} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=4=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

Also, according to the rank-nullity theorem, if $A$ is a matrix with $n$ columns, then 

$$
\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A)=n.
$$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is false. Since the generating vectors in 

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\text{Span}\{[\begin{aligned}5 \\ -2 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\}
$$

are linearly independent, we conclude that the number of non-pivot columns in $A$ is equal to $2.$

- Statement II is false. Since $\text{nullity}(A)=2\ne 0,$ then by the invertible matrix theorem, we have $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{4}.$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for the matrix $A,$ the number of columns is $n=4.$ Now, according to the rank-nullity theorem, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{rank}(A)+\text{nullity}(A) & =n \\ \text{rank}(A)+2 & =4 \\ \text{rank}(A) & =4-2 \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

Which of the following augmented matrices are in row echelon form?

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}
	\right]
$$

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 2 & -1 & 5 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 7\end{array}
	\right]
$$

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 0 & -1 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{array}
	\right]
$$

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}0 & 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}
	\right].
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.

- Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

With that in mind, let's look at each matrix in turn.

- The first matrix is not in row echelon form since $a_{32} \neq 0$ (condition II is violated).

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 2 & -1 & 0 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 0 & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{red}1} & 1 & 1\end{array}
	\right]
$$

- The second matrix is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 2 & -1 & 5 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 0 & -2 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 7\end{array}
	\right]
$$

- The third matrix is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 0 & -1 & 4 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 0 & 1 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & 0\end{array}
	\right]
$$

- The fourth matrix is not in row echelon form since, for example, the leading entry $a_{22}$ lies to the left of the leading entry $a_{13}$ (condition II is violated).

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Operations That Would Transform a Matrix To Row Echelon Form

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Let's consider our matrices $A$ and $B$ once more, with the leading entries highlighted.

![](images/af/af61f32297e248ab9989ba59ea6c9bda2f99efe19d25df525fef916617843a32.svg)

We say that a matrix is in **row echelon form** if it satisfies the following conditions:

I. All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.

II. Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

Here, $B$ is in row echelon form since both conditions are satisfied. However, $A$ is not in row echelon form since condition II is violated: the leading entry of the third row $(a_{32}={\color{red}1})$ is placed just below the leading entry of the second row $(a_{22}=3).$

Generally speaking, row echelon form means that we have *stairs* where each step (represented by a leading entry $\bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\large\ast}$) has a height of $1.$

![](images/67/67f83c454e59d16ae80cf67a19b19f968182251a2e5d1b405e2c422e0313d5b7.png)

Finally, an *augmented* matrix is in row echelon form if the coefficient matrix (i.e., the part that is to the left of the vertical bar) is in row echelon form.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
What is the sum of the leading entries of the $1$st, $3$rd and $4$th rows in the matrix $A,$ given below?

$$

The first non-zero entry of each row (from left to right) is the leading entry. 

Therefore, the leading entries of the $1$st, $3$rd and $4$th rows of $A$ are $-1$, $-4$ and $8$, respectively.

$$

So, the answer is $-1+(-4)+8=3.$

	\right].
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Remember that an augmented matrix is in row echelon form if its coefficient matrix satisfies the following conditions:

- All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.

	\right]
$$

- The second matrix is in row echelon form (both conditions are satisfied).

$$
\left[
	\begin{array}{ccc|c}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 2 & -1 & 5 \\ {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} & 0 & -2 \\ {\color{blue}0} & {\color{blue}0} & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{1} & 7\end{array}

$$

	\right]
$$

- The fourth matrix is not in row echelon form since, for example, the leading entry $a_{22}$ lies to the left of the leading entry $a_{13}$ (condition II is violated).

$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Let's consider our matrices $A$ and $B$ once more, with the leading entries highlighted.

![](images/af/af61f32297e248ab9989ba59ea6c9bda2f99efe19d25df525fef916617843a32.svg)

We say that a matrix is in **row echelon form** if it satisfies the following conditions:

I. All the zero rows (rows with only zeros), if any, are placed at the *bottom* of the matrix.

II. Each leading entry of a row is in a column *to the right* of the leading entry of the row above it.

Here, $B$ is in row echelon form since both conditions are satisfied. However, $A$ is not in row echelon form since condition II is violated: the leading entry of the third row $(a_{32}={\color{red}1})$ is placed just below the leading entry of the second row $(a_{22}=3).$

Generally speaking, row echelon form means that we have *stairs* where each step (represented by a leading entry $\bbox[lightgray, 3pt]{\large\ast}$) has a height of $1.$

![](images/67/67f83c454e59d16ae80cf67a19b19f968182251a2e5d1b405e2c422e0313d5b7.png)

Finally, an *augmented* matrix is in row echelon form if the coefficient matrix (i.e., the part that is to the left of the vertical bar) is in row echelon form.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
What is the sum of the leading entries of the $1$st, $3$rd and $4$th rows in the matrix $A,$ given below?

$$
A=
\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 & 8 \\ 0 & -4 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & 8 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The first non-zero entry of each row (from left to right) is the leading entry. 

Therefore, the leading entries of the $1$st, $3$rd and $4$th rows of $A$ are $-1$, $-4$ and $8$, respectively.

$$
A
=\begin{bmatrix}\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{-1} & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 7 & 8 \\ 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{-4} & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 0 & \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{8} & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

So, the answer is $-1+(-4)+8=3.$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Remember that the **identity matrix** $I_n$ is an $n \times n$ square matrix with $1$'s on the diagonal, and where all other elements are $0.$ For example, the $3 \times 3$ identity matrix $I_3$ is given below: $$ \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} $$ The identity matrix gets its name from the fact that whenever we multiply a matrix by the corresponding identity matrix, the matrix remains unchanged. For example, let's consider the matrix
$A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 10 \\ 6 & -2 & 2 \\ 23 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}$
Multiplying the matrix $A$ by the identity matrix $I_3,$ we find that the result is just $A$ itself: $$ \begin{aligned}A\cdot {I}_{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 10 \\ 6 & -2 & 2 \\ 23 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}(-2)\cdot 1+3\cdot 0+10\cdot 0 & (-2)\cdot 0+3\cdot 1+10\cdot 0 & (-2)\cdot 0+3\cdot 0+10\cdot 1 \\ 6\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 0+2\cdot 0 & 6\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0 & 6\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot 0+2\cdot 1 \\ 23\cdot 1+4\cdot 0+8\cdot 0 & 23\cdot 0+4\cdot 1+8\cdot 0 & 23\cdot 0+4\cdot 0+8\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 10 \\ 6 & -2 & 2 \\ 23 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} \\ & =A\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $A \cdot I_3 = A.$ You can check that $I_3 \cdot A = A$ using the same method. This result holds in general: > For *any* square $n \times n$ matrix $A,$ we have > > > $$ > A \cdot I_n = I_n \cdot A = A. > $$ In other words, the $n \times n$ identity matrix $I_n$ has a similar property to the number $1,$ namely that $$ a\cdot 1 = 1\cdot a = a $$ for any real number $a.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Multiplying a Matrix by the Identity Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Whenever we multiply a matrix $A$ by the $n$th column of the identity matrix, the result is the $n$th column of $A.$ For example, consider the matrix
$A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
The first column of the identity matrix $I_2$ is given by $$ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ If we multiply $A$ by the column on the *right*, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 1\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ The product is just the first column of the matrix $A.$ Using the same method, you can check for yourself that when we multiply $A$ by the second column of $I_2,$ the result is the second column of $A.$ On the other hand, if we multiply $A$ by the first *row* of the identity matrix $I_2$ on the *left*, we will obtain the first row of $A$. Indeed, $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+1\cdot 0 & (-1)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Multiplying a Matrix by a Column or Row of the Identity Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We've been using the fact that $AI_n = I_n A = A$ for any $n \times n$ matrix $A.$ But how do we know for sure?

Let's prove the case of $n=2.$ That is, let's prove that $AI_2=I_2A = A,$ where $A$ is any $2\times2$ matrix.

Any general $2 \times 2$ matrix can be written as
$\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ 

Then, multiplying by $I_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A{I}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11}\cdot 1+{a}_{12}\cdot 0 & {a}_{11}\cdot 0+{a}_{12}\cdot 1 \\ {a}_{21}\cdot 1+{a}_{22}\cdot 0 & {a}_{21}\cdot 0+{a}_{22}\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

The above proof shows that the property $A I_2 = I_2 A = A$ holds for all $2\times2$ matrices $A.$

In general, to prove that the property $AI_n = I_n A = A$ holds for all $n \times n$ matrices $A,$ we can use the same method.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Remember that the **identity matrix** $I_n$ is an $n \times n$ square matrix with $1$'s on the diagonal, and where all other elements are $0.$ For example, the $3 \times 3$ identity matrix $I_3$ is given below: $$ \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} $$ The identity matrix gets its name from the fact that whenever we multiply a matrix by the corresponding identity matrix, the matrix remains unchanged. For example, let's consider the matrix
$A=\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 10 \\ 6 & -2 & 2 \\ 23 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}$
Multiplying the matrix $A$ by the identity matrix $I_3,$ we find that the result is just $A$ itself: $$ \begin{aligned}A\cdot {I}_{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 10 \\ 6 & -2 & 2 \\ 23 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}(-2)\cdot 1+3\cdot 0+10\cdot 0 & (-2)\cdot 0+3\cdot 1+10\cdot 0 & (-2)\cdot 0+3\cdot 0+10\cdot 1 \\ 6\cdot 1+(-2)\cdot 0+2\cdot 0 & 6\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0 & 6\cdot 0+(-2)\cdot 0+2\cdot 1 \\ 23\cdot 1+4\cdot 0+8\cdot 0 & 23\cdot 0+4\cdot 1+8\cdot 0 & 23\cdot 0+4\cdot 0+8\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 3 & 10 \\ 6 & -2 & 2 \\ 23 & 4 & 8\end{bmatrix} \\ & =A\end{aligned} $$ Therefore, $A \cdot I_3 = A.$ You can check that $I_3 \cdot A = A$ using the same method. This result holds in general: > For *any* square $n \times n$ matrix $A,$ we have > > > $$ > A \cdot I_n = I_n \cdot A = A. > $$ In other words, the $n \times n$ identity matrix $I_n$ has a similar property to the number $1,$ namely that $$ a\cdot 1 = 1\cdot a = a $$ for any real number $a.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Multiplying a Matrix by the Identity Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Whenever we multiply a matrix $A$ by the $n$th column of the identity matrix, the result is the $n$th column of $A.$ For example, consider the matrix
$A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
The first column of the identity matrix $I_2$ is given by $$ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ If we multiply $A$ by the column on the *right*, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 1\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ The product is just the first column of the matrix $A.$ Using the same method, you can check for yourself that when we multiply $A$ by the second column of $I_2,$ the result is the second column of $A.$ On the other hand, if we multiply $A$ by the first *row* of the identity matrix $I_2$ on the *left*, we will obtain the first row of $A$. Indeed, $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+1\cdot 0 & (-1)\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Multiplying a Matrix by a Column or Row of the Identity Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We've been using the fact that $AI_n = I_n A = A$ for any $n \times n$ matrix $A.$ But how do we know for sure?

Let's prove the case of $n=2.$ That is, let's prove that $AI_2=I_2A = A,$ where $A$ is any $2\times2$ matrix.

Any general $2 \times 2$ matrix can be written as
$\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ 

Then, multiplying by $I_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A{I}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11}\cdot 1+{a}_{12}\cdot 0 & {a}_{11}\cdot 0+{a}_{12}\cdot 1 \\ {a}_{21}\cdot 1+{a}_{22}\cdot 0 & {a}_{21}\cdot 0+{a}_{22}\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

The above proof shows that the property $A I_2 = I_2 A = A$ holds for all $2\times2$ matrices $A.$

In general, to prove that the property $AI_n = I_n A = A$ holds for all $n \times n$ matrices $A,$ we can use the same method.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Whenever we multiply a matrix $A$ by the $n$th column of the identity matrix, the result is the $n$th column of $A.$ For example, consider the matrix
$A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
The first column of the identity matrix $I_2$ is given by $$ \begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} $$ If we multiply $A$ by the column on the *right*, we get $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 1+(-1)\cdot 0 \\ 1\cdot 1+2\cdot 0\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 1\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned} $$ The product is just the first column of the matrix $A.$ Using the same method, you can check for yourself that when we multiply $A$ by the second column of $I_2,$ the result is the second column of $A.$ On the other hand, if we multiply $A$ by the first *row* of the identity matrix $I_2$ on the *left*, we will obtain the first row of $A$. We've been using the fact that $AI_n = I_n A = A$ for any $n \times n$ matrix $A.$ But how do we know for sure?

Let's prove the case of $n=2.$ That is, let's prove that $AI_2=I_2A = A,$ where $A$ is any $2\times2$ matrix.

Any general $2 \times 2$ matrix can be written as
$\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}$ 

Then, multiplying by $I_2,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A{I}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11}\cdot 1+{a}_{12}\cdot 0 & {a}_{11}\cdot 0+{a}_{12}\cdot 1 \\ {a}_{21}\cdot 1+{a}_{22}\cdot 0 & {a}_{21}\cdot 0+{a}_{22}\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

The above proof shows that the property $A I_2 = I_2 A = A$ holds for all $2\times2$ matrices $A.$

In general, to prove that the property $AI_n = I_n A = A$ holds for all $n \times n$ matrices $A,$ we can use the same method.

\begin{aligned}A{I}_{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11}\cdot 1+{a}_{12}\cdot 0 & {a}_{11}\cdot 0+{a}_{12}\cdot 1 \\ {a}_{21}\cdot 1+{a}_{22}\cdot 0 & {a}_{21}\cdot 0+{a}_{22}\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

Similarly,

$$
\begin{aligned}{I}_{2}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22}\end{bmatrix} \\  & =A.\end{aligned}
$$

The above proof shows that the property $A I_2 = I_2 A = A$ holds for all $2\times2$ matrices $A.$

In general, to prove that the property $AI_n = I_n A = A$ holds for all $n \times n$ matrices $A,$ we can use the same method.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
If $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are three matrices that are conformable for multiplication, then they follow the **associative law**:

$$
\left( AB\right) C = A\left( BC\right)
$$

So, when we wish to compute a product $ABC,$ we don't always have to start by multiplying $AB.$ Alternatively, we can start by multiplying $BC,$ and then multiply $A$ by the result. 

Sometimes rearranging the parentheses might make the computations slightly easier.

$$
ABC = (AB)C = A(BC).
$$

Notice that $A$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix, $B$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix, and $C$ is a $3 \times 1$ matrix. Therefore, 

- multiplying $A$ by $B$, we will obtain a $3 \times 3$ matrix that will require finding $9$ entries, while

- multiplying $B$ by $C$, we will obtain a $3 \times 1$ matrix that will require finding only $3$ entries.

So, we find the product $BC$ first:

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 5 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ -4 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 0 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply $A$ by $BC\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}ABC & =A(BC) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 0 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -4 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Given that $A, B,$ and $C$ are $6 \times 6$ matrices, which of the following statements are always true?

I. $A(BC) = (AB)C$

II. $A(B+C) = BA+CA$

III. $A(B+C) = AB+AC$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's consider the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. Matrix multiplication is associative, so $(AB)C = A(BC)$ in general.

- Statement II is false. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $A(B+C) = AB + AC$ in general. However, since matrix multiplication is not commutative, we have

$$
AB + AC  \neq BA + CA.
$$

- Statement III is true. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $(A+B)C = AC+BC,$ and $A(B+C) = AB+AC$ in general.

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Given that $A$ and $B$  are $8\times 8$ matrices,  and ${I}_{8}$ is the $8\times 8$ identity matrix,  which of the following statements are always true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A{I}_{8}={I}_{8}A$
- **II.** $AB=BA$
- **III.** $A\cdot 2{I}_{8}=2A$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Let's consider the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. Matrix multiplication is not commutative in general, however, multiplication by the identity matrix is always commutative. In this case, we have  $A{I}_{8}={I}_{8}A=A.$

- Statement II is false. Matrix multiplication is not commutative, so $AB\ne BA$ in general.

- Statement III is true. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so 

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cdot 2{I}_{8} & =A({I}_{8}+{I}_{8}) \\  & =A{I}_{8}+A{I}_{8} \\  & =A+A \\  & =2A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only statements I  and III are true.

Notice that $A$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix, $B$ is a $2\times 1$ matrix, and $C$ is a $1\times 3$ matrix. Therefore, 

- multiplying $A$ by $B$, we will obtain a $1\times 1$ matrix, which will require finding only $1$ entry, while

- multiplying $B$ by $C$, we will obtain a $2\times 3$ matrix, which will require finding $6$ entries.

So, we find the product $AB$ first: 

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}4 \\ -6\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0\cdot 4+(-3)\cdot (-6)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0+18\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}18\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply $(AB)$ by $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}ABC & =(AB)\,C \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}18\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}54 & 0 & 72\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement I is true. Matrix multiplication is associative, so $(AB)C = A(BC)$ in general.

$$

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we are given a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} &=-2 \\ 5{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1\end{aligned}
$$

We can apply some operations to the augmented matrix that do not change the set of solutions for the corresponding system. These operations are called **elementary row operations**. 

After applying an **elementary row operation** to the augmented matrix, the new corresponding system will have the same solutions.

There are three types of elementary row operations:

- switching any two rows: 

$$
R_i \leftrightarrow R_j
$$

- multiplying (each element of) a row by a non-zero number: 

$$
R_i := k R_i,\qquad k \neq 0
$$

- adding a multiple of one row to another row: 

$$
R_j := R_j+k R_i,\qquad j \neq i
$$

In the notations above, the "$:=$" symbol is called the **assignment operator.** We use this to assign new values to every element of a given row.

For example, the row operation $R_1 := 2 R_1$ means, "create a new row $1$ by taking the old row $1$ and multiplying it by $2.$" When we do this, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 4 & -2 \\ 5 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right]\,{R}_{1}:=2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 3 & 2\cdot (-1) & 2\cdot 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 4 & -2 \\ 5 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 4 & -2 \\ 5 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

A few final points on notation.

- We use the similarity symbol ($\sim$) to indicate when one matrix is transformed into another matrix using elementary row operations.

- The assignment operator $:=$ is sometimes called the "walrus operator" because it looks like a walrus on its side!

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Consider the matrix $A,$ given by

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The operation $R_2:=R_2 + (-4) R_1$ means that we need to add $-4$ times the first row to the second row. 

Carrying out this row operation, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 2 & -1 \\ 7 & 12 & 13\end{bmatrix}\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-4)\cdot {R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 4+(-4)(1) & 2+(-4)(2) & -1+(-4)(3) \\ 7 & 12 & 13\end{bmatrix} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 & 3 \\ 0 & -6 & -13 \\ 7 & 12 & 13\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}C & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 4 & 7 \\ 5 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\,{R}_{1}:={R}_{1}+(-2)\cdot {R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}0+(-2)(5) & 4+(-2)(2) & 7+(-2)(1) \\ 5 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-10 & 0 & 5 \\ 5 & 2 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}\,{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(1)\cdot {R}_{2} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-10 & 0 & 5 \\ 5 & 2 & 1 \\ 1+(1)(5) & 3+(1)(2) & 0+(1)(1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-10 & 0 & 5 \\ 5 & 2 & 1 \\ 6 & 5 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which elementary row operation could transform the matrix $A$ into the matrix $B$, where 

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 4 \\ 4 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
B=\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 6 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, notice that the $1$st and the $3$rd rows are the same in both matrices. The only row that has been changed is the $2$nd row. 

Now, applying the operation $R_2:=R_2+1 \cdot R_1,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 4 \\ 4 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+1\cdot {R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 4 \\ 4+1\cdot (-4) & 1+1\cdot (-2) & 2+1\cdot 4 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}-4 & -2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 6 \\ 1 & 2 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =B\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the transformation could be done by the operation 

$$
R_2:=R_2+1\cdot R_1
$$

or simply

$$
R_2:=R_2+R_1.
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Given that

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 5 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

 which elementary row operation could make $a_{22}=0?$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
In the given matrix, we have $a_{22}=5$ and we want to perform an elementary row operation that makes $a_{22}=0.$

- We *cannot* make $a_{22}=0$ by switching two rows, because there are no rows with $0$ as the second entry.

- We *cannot* multiply the second row by $0,$ because we are only allowed to multiply rows by *nonzero* constants.

- However, we *can* add a multiple of another row to the $2$nd row to make $a_{22}=0.$

Looking at the first row, we see that $a_{12}=1.$ If we add $-5$ times this entry to $a_{22},$ we will get $a_{22}=0$ as desired. So, the elementary row operation that we need to use is

$$
R_2 := R_2 + (-5) \cdot R_1.
$$

Applying this operation, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 5 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-5)\cdot {R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -2 \\ -1+(-5)\cdot 3 & 5+(-5)\cdot 1 & 6+(-5)\cdot (-2) \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -2 \\ -16 & 0 & 16 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the desired elemetary row operation is

$$
R_2 := R_2 + (-5) \cdot R_1,
$$

or simply

$$
R_2 := R_2 -5 R_1.
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying the Appropriate Row Operation To Transform a Given Entry to a Desired Value

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we are given a system of linear equations and its respective augmented matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}-{x}_{3} &=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+4{x}_{3} &=-2 \\ 5{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} &=1\end{aligned}
$$

We can apply some operations to the augmented matrix that do not change the set of solutions for the corresponding system. These operations are called **elementary row operations**. 

After applying an **elementary row operation** to the augmented matrix, the new corresponding system will have the same solutions.

There are three types of elementary row operations:

- switching any two rows: 

$$
R_i \leftrightarrow R_j
$$

- multiplying (each element of) a row by a non-zero number: 

$$
R_i := k R_i,\qquad k \neq 0
$$

- adding a multiple of one row to another row: 

$$
R_j := R_j+k R_i,\qquad j \neq i
$$

In the notations above, the "$:=$" symbol is called the **assignment operator.** We use this to assign new values to every element of a given row.

For example, the row operation $R_1 := 2 R_1$ means, "create a new row $1$ by taking the old row $1$ and multiplying it by $2.$" When we do this, we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & ∼\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1 & 3 & -1 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 4 & -2 \\ 5 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{array}\right]\,{R}_{1}:=2{R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 3 & 2\cdot (-1) & 2\cdot 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 4 & -2 \\ 5 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 & -2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 4 & -2 \\ 5 & 1 & 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

A few final points on notation.

- We use the similarity symbol ($\sim$) to indicate when one matrix is transformed into another matrix using elementary row operations.

- The assignment operator $:=$ is sometimes called the "walrus operator" because it looks like a walrus on its side!

In the given matrix, we have $a_{22}=5$ and we want to perform an elementary row operation that makes $a_{22}=0.$

- We *cannot* multiply the second row by $0,$ because we are only allowed to multiply rows by *nonzero* constants.

- However, we *can* add a multiple of another row to the $2$nd row to make $a_{22}=0.$

$$
R_2 := R_2 + (-5) \cdot R_1.
$$

Applying this operation, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 5 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-5)\cdot {R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -2 \\ -1+(-5)\cdot 3 & 5+(-5)\cdot 1 & 6+(-5)\cdot (-2) \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -2 \\ -16 & 0 & 16 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the desired elemetary row operation is

$$
R_2 := R_2 + (-5) \cdot R_1,

or simply

$$

17592186059583.:question/problem:
Given that

$$
A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 5 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}
$$

 which elementary row operation could make $a_{22}=0?$
17592186059583.:question/worked-solution:
In the given matrix, we have $a_{22}=5$ and we want to perform an elementary row operation that makes $a_{22}=0.$

- We *cannot* make $a_{22}=0$ by switching two rows, because there are no rows with $0$ as the second entry.

- We *cannot* multiply the second row by $0,$ because we are only allowed to multiply rows by *nonzero* constants.

- However, we *can* add a multiple of another row to the $2$nd row to make $a_{22}=0.$

Looking at the first row, we see that $a_{12}=1.$ If we add $-5$ times this entry to $a_{22},$ we will get $a_{22}=0$ as desired. So, the elementary row operation that we need to use is

$$
R_2 := R_2 + (-5) \cdot R_1.
$$

Applying this operation, we obtain the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -2 \\ -1 & 5 & 6 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\,{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-5)\cdot {R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -2 \\ -1+(-5)\cdot 3 & 5+(-5)\cdot 1 & 6+(-5)\cdot (-2) \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 1 & -2 \\ -16 & 0 & 16 \\ 0 & 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the desired elemetary row operation is

$$
R_2 := R_2 + (-5) \cdot R_1,
$$

or simply

$$
R_2 := R_2 -5 R_1.
$$
