:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Given the scalar $a,$ the **multiplicative inverse** of $a$ is defined as the scalar $a^{-1}$ such that $$ a \cdot a^{-1} = a^{-1} \cdot a = 1. $$ For example, the multiplicative inverse of $2$ is the number $2^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ because $$ \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2 = 2\cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 1. $$ Similarly, given a square $n \times n$ matrix $A,$ the **inverse** of $A$ is defined as the $n \times n$ matrix $A^{-1}$ such that $$ A \cdot A^{-1} = A^{-1} \cdot A = I_n, $$ where $I_n$ is the $n\times n$ identity matrix. For example, suppose we're given the following $2\times 2$ matrix:
$A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
The inverse of the above matrix is given by $$ \begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} $$ To verify that the above matrix is in fact the inverse of $A,$ first observe that if we multiply $A$ by the above matrix $A^{-1},$ then we get the identity matrix $I_2\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1\cdot (-2)+(-1)\cdot 1 & -1\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1 \\ 1\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 1 & 1\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned} $$ Likewise, if we multiply $A^{-1}$ by $A,$ then we also get the identity matrix $I_2\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A} & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned} $$ We do not yet know how to find the inverse of a matrix. However, we can verify that one matrix is the inverse of the other by carrying out the same procedure as we did here.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Using the method of direct verification, determine whether the matrix $B$ is the inverse of $A,$ where
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
$B=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We must check whether $AB = BA = I_2.$

Computing $AB,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={I}_{2}.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Likewise, computing $BA,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}BA & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ -1 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={I}_{2}.\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $B = A^{-1}.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Determining the Inverse of a Larger Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The number $0$ does not have an inverse for multiplication over the real numbers, because there's no such number $a$ that $a \cdot 0 = 1.$ Instead, for every $a$ we have $a \cdot 0 = 0.$

Similarly, not every matrix has an inverse.

- If a matrix is not square, an inverse does not exist.

- Some square matrices do not have an inverse. If a square matrix does not have an inverse, then it is said to be **singular**. An example of a singular matrix is the zero matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

We will soon learn how to calculate the inverse of a square matrix, and we'll also soon learn how to determine when a square matrix does not have an inverse.

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Determining the Inverse of a Larger Matrix

17592186049125.:topic/title: Introduction to the Inverse of a Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Given the scalar $a,$ the **multiplicative inverse** of $a$ is defined as the scalar $a^{-1}$ such that $$ a \cdot a^{-1} = a^{-1} \cdot a = 1. $$ For example, the multiplicative inverse of $2$ is the number $2^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ because $$ \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2 = 2\cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 1. $$ Similarly, given a square $n \times n$ matrix $A,$ the **inverse** of $A$ is defined as the $n \times n$ matrix $A^{-1}$ such that $$ A \cdot A^{-1} = A^{-1} \cdot A = I_n, $$ where $I_n$ is the $n\times n$ identity matrix. For example, suppose we're given the following $2\times 2$ matrix:
$A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
The inverse of the above matrix is given by $$ \begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} $$ To verify that the above matrix is in fact the inverse of $A,$ first observe that if we multiply $A$ by the above matrix $A^{-1},$ then we get the identity matrix $I_2\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1\cdot (-2)+(-1)\cdot 1 & -1\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1 \\ 1\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 1 & 1\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned} $$ Likewise, if we multiply $A^{-1}$ by $A,$ then we also get the identity matrix $I_2\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A} & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned} $$ We do not yet know how to find the inverse of a matrix. However, we can verify that one matrix is the inverse of the other by carrying out the same procedure as we did here.

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Determining the Inverse of a Larger Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The number $0$ does not have an inverse for multiplication over the real numbers, because there's no such number $a$ that $a \cdot 0 = 1.$ Instead, for every $a$ we have $a \cdot 0 = 0.$

Similarly, not every matrix has an inverse.

- If a matrix is not square, an inverse does not exist.

- Some square matrices do not have an inverse. If a square matrix does not have an inverse, then it is said to be **singular**. An example of a singular matrix is the zero matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

We will soon learn how to calculate the inverse of a square matrix, and we'll also soon learn how to determine when a square matrix does not have an inverse.
:step/content.:tutorial/title: Not Every Matrix Has an Inverse

17592186087930.:activity/title: Introduction to the Inverse of a Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Given the scalar $a,$ the **multiplicative inverse** of $a$ is defined as the scalar $a^{-1}$ such that $$ a \cdot a^{-1} = a^{-1} \cdot a = 1. $$ For example, the multiplicative inverse of $2$ is the number $2^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ because $$ \dfrac{1}{2}\cdot 2 = 2\cdot \dfrac{1}{2} = 1. $$ Similarly, given a square $n \times n$ matrix $A,$ the **inverse** of $A$ is defined as the $n \times n$ matrix $A^{-1}$ such that $$ A \cdot A^{-1} = A^{-1} \cdot A = I_n, $$ where $I_n$ is the $n\times n$ identity matrix. For example, suppose we're given the following $2\times 2$ matrix:
$A=\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
The inverse of the above matrix is given by $$ \begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix} $$ To verify that the above matrix is in fact the inverse of $A,$ first observe that if we multiply $A$ by the above matrix $A^{-1},$ then we get the identity matrix $I_2\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A}{{\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{{A}^{-1}} & =\begin{bmatrix}-1\cdot (-2)+(-1)\cdot 1 & -1\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1 \\ 1\cdot (-2)+2\cdot 1 & 1\cdot (-1)+2\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\ & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned} $$ Likewise, if we multiply $A^{-1}$ by $A,$ then we also get the identity matrix $I_2\mathbin{:}$ $$ \begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}{{\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}}_{⏟}}_{A} & ={I}_{2}\,✓\end{aligned} $$ We do not yet know how to find the inverse of a matrix. However, we can verify that one matrix is the inverse of the other by carrying out the same procedure as we did here.

The number $0$ does not have an inverse for multiplication over the real numbers, because there's no such number $a$ that $a \cdot 0 = 1.$ Instead, for every $a$ we have $a \cdot 0 = 0.$

Similarly, not every matrix has an inverse.

- If a matrix is not square, an inverse does not exist.

- Some square matrices do not have an inverse. If a square matrix does not have an inverse, then it is said to be **singular**. An example of a singular matrix is the zero matrix

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

We will soon learn how to calculate the inverse of a square matrix, and we'll also soon learn how to determine when a square matrix does not have an inverse.

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Symmetric Matrices

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose that $A$ is a symmetric matrix. Then, we have the following properties:

- $-A$ is symmetric

- $A^m$ is symmetric for any positive integer $m$

- $A^{-1}$ is symmetric for nonsingular $A$

If $A$ and $B$ are $n\times n$ symmetric matrices, we have the following properties:

- $A+B$ is symmetric

- The product $A\cdot B$ is *not* always symmetric. For example, if 
![](images/e4/e41d28b6c6562ada530024fe6ab29cc16447dce14b2f741b8b35758618c78103.svg)
then the product $A\cdot B$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cdot B & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\,\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

 
which is *not* symmetric.

Finally, the following two properties can be used to construct symmetric matrices:

- $A + A^T$ is symmetric for any *square* matrix $A$

- $A^T A$ and $A A^T$ are symmetric for *any* matrix $A$

The last property is true for *any* $m\times n$ matrix. This property is particularly useful, as we'll discover in future lessons.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. If $A$ is *any* $n\times n$ matrix, then $A+A^T$ is always symmetric.

II. The difference between two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is symmetric.

III. The product of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is symmetric.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A = A^T
$$

Equivalently, $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+{A}^{T})^{T} & ={A}^{T}+({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}+A \\  & =A+{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the sum or difference between two symmetric matrices is symmetric.

- Statement III is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 
![](images/81/812e9888b920e0338fd72116464b8b96c8c272f95f180cd46aa3f1db9afac8d2.svg)
Their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. If $A$ is *any* $n\times n$ matrix, then $A+A^T$ is always symmetric.

II. The difference between two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is symmetric.

III. The product of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is symmetric.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A = A^T
$$

Equivalently, $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+{A}^{T})^{T} & ={A}^{T}+({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}+A \\  & =A+{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the sum or difference between two symmetric matrices is symmetric.

- Statement III is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 
![](images/81/812e9888b920e0338fd72116464b8b96c8c272f95f180cd46aa3f1db9afac8d2.svg)
Their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrix 

$\,$ $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

However, ${A}^{2}$ is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 

$\,$ $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,B=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

However, their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any non-singular symmetric matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}({A}^{-1})^{T} & =({A}^{T})^{-1} \\  & ={A}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We add two matrices by adding the corresponding entries. We can only do this if they have the same number of rows and columns, that is, they have the same dimensions.

For example, consider the matrices

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix},\qquad B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We see that both $A$ and $B$ are $2\times 2$ matrices, so we can add them. The sum ${A} + {B}\,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}A+B & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+1 & 3+0 \\ 2+0 & 4+(-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, the sum of two matrices is another matrix with the same dimensions.

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Adding Non-Square Matrices

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We add two matrices by adding the corresponding entries. We can only do this if they have the same number of rows and columns, that is, they have the same dimensions.

For example, consider the matrices

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix},\qquad B = \begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We see that both $A$ and $B$ are $2\times 2$ matrices, so we can add them. The sum ${A} + {B}\,$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}A+B & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+1 & 3+0 \\ 2+0 & 4+(-1)\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 2 & 3\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, the sum of two matrices is another matrix with the same dimensions.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We can multiply matrices by numbers. This type of multiplication is known as **scalar multiplication**. Here, a **scalar** is just a number.

For example, consider the matrix

$$
{A}=
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To multiply ${A}$ by the scalar $2,$ we just multiply each entry of ${A}$ by $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2A & =2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 3 \\ 2\cdot 2 & 2\cdot 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In general, to multiply a $m \times n$ matrix $A$ by a scalar $c,$ we multiply each entry of $A$ by $c$ as follows:

$$
cA 
	=
	c \cdot
	\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} & … & {a}_{1n} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22} & … & {a}_{2n} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ {a}_{m1} & {a}_{m2} & … & {a}_{mn}\end{bmatrix} 
	= 
	\begin{bmatrix}c{a}_{11} & c{a}_{12} & … & c{a}_{1n} \\ c{a}_{21} & c{a}_{22} & … & c{a}_{2n} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ c{a}_{m1} & c{a}_{m2} & … & c{a}_{mn}\end{bmatrix}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
If 

$$
k {A} =
\begin{bmatrix}
        	1 & 3 & 4  \\
        	6 & 0 & -2
    	\end{bmatrix},
$$

where 

$$
{A} =
\begin{bmatrix}
        	2 & 6 & 8  \\
        	12 & 0 & -4
    	\end{bmatrix}
$$

and $k$ is a scalar, calculate the value of $k.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To express $kA,$ we multiply each entry of $A$ by $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}kA & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 & 8 \\ 12 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2k & 6k & 8k \\ 12k & 0 & -4k\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the above result equal to the matrix given for $kA$ in the problem statement:

$$
\left\lbrack
    	\begin{matrix}
        	2k & 6k & 8k  \\
        	12k & 0 & -4k
    	\end{matrix}
    	\right\rbrack
=
\left\lbrack
    	\begin{matrix}
        	1 & 3 & 4  \\
        	6 & 0 & -2
    	\end{matrix}
    	\right\rbrack
$$

We can solve for $k$ by equating any two corresponding (nonzero) elements. Let's choose the top-left elements, $2k$ and $1.$ Equating these elements, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2k & =1 \\ k & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** We would still get the same result if we chose any other two corresponding (nonzero) elements.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Calculate $2A+\frac{1}{2}B$, where
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
$B=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We multiply each entry of $A$ by $2$ and each entry of $B$ by $\dfrac{1}{2},$ and then add the resulting matrices, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2A+\frac{1}{2}B & =2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 5 \\ 2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0 & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2 \\ \frac{1}{2}\cdot 4 & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 10 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2+0 & 10+1 \\ 2+2 & 4+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 11 \\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Calculate $2H-3L$, where
$H=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}$
and
$L=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We multiply each entry of $H$ by $2$ and each entry of $L$ by $3,$ and then subtract the resulting matrices, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2H-3L & =2\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 3 & 2\cdot (-2) \\ 2\cdot 2 & 2\cdot (-1)\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 0 & 3\cdot 1 \\ 3\cdot 2 & 3\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6-0 & -4-3 \\ 4-6 & -2-3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -7 \\ -2 & -5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating a Linear Combination of Two Matrices

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Since scalar multiplication is done entry-wise, it obeys the same kind of rules as multiplication of real numbers.

For example, for any numbers $c_1, c_2$ and any matrix $A,$ we can perform scalar multiplication in any order: 

$$
c_1 (c_2 A) = (c_1 c_2) A = c_2 (c_1 A)
$$

Moreover, we can distribute a matrix over the sum or difference of scalars:

$$
(c_1 \pm c_2)A = c_1A \pm c_2A
$$

We can also distribute scalar multiplication over the sum or difference of two matrices:

$$
c (A \pm B) = c A \pm c B
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}2A+\frac{1}{2}B & =2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 5 \\ 2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0 & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2 \\ \frac{1}{2}\cdot 4 & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 10 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2+0 & 10+1 \\ 2+2 & 4+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 11 \\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we are given an $n \!\times\! n$ invertible matrix $A.$ Remember that if $A$ is invertible, then the equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.$

Let's extract all possible information from this fact using the vector spaces related to the matrix, namely, the *column space* and the *null space*.

- The fact that the unique solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ is $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ tells us that 

$$
\textrm{Null}(A)=\{ \mathbf{0} \},
$$

 or alternatively, 

$$
\textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \textrm{nullity}(A)=0.
$$

- Furthermore, if $\textrm{dim(Null}(A))=0$ then $A$ has no *non-pivot* columns, or equivalently, all the columns of $A$ are *pivot columns*. So 

$$
\textrm{dim(Col}(A))=\textrm{rank}(A)=n.
$$

- Finally, since $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its basis has $n$ linearly independent vectors, we can conclude that 

$$
\textrm{Col}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n.
$$

All the results mentioned above can be summarized in the following theorem, called the **invertible matrix theorem**:

*Let $A$ be an $n \!\times\! n$ matrix. Then we have the following equivalence:*

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\{\begin{bmatrix}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ -{x}_{1} \\ 2{x}_{2}\end{bmatrix}\,|\,{x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R\}?
$$

I. $\text{dim(Null}(A))\ne 0$

II. $A$ is invertible

III. $\text{Col}(A)={R}^{4}$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Since $A$ is a $4\times 4$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{4} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=4=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true. Since 

$$
\text{Null}(A)=\{{x}_{1}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 0 \\ -1 \\ 0\end{bmatrix}+{x}_{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{bmatrix}\,|\,{x}_{1},{x}_{2}\in R\}
$$

we conclude that 

$$
\text{dim(Null}(A))=2\ne 0.
$$

- Statement II is false. Since $\text{dim(Null}(A))\ne 0,$ then according to the invertible matrix theorem, the matrix $A$ can't be invertible.

- Statement III is false. Since $A$ is not invertible, then by the invertible matrix theorem, we must have $\text{Col}(A)\ne {R}^{4}.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

III. $A$ has $4$ pivot columns

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{3} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=3=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. 

- Statement I is false. Indeed,   a matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ Since here we have $det(A)=-1\ne 0,$ our matrix $A$ must be invertible.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, by the invertible matrix theorem
$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\text{rank}(A)=3.$

- Statement III is false. Since $\text{rank}(A)=3$,  it must be $\text{dim(Col}(A))=3$ which, in turn, means that  $A$ has $3$ pivot columns, not $4.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we are given an $n \!\times\! n$ invertible matrix $A.$ Remember that if $A$ is invertible, then the equation $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.$

Let's extract all possible information from this fact using the vector spaces related to the matrix, namely, the *column space* and the *null space*.

- The fact that the unique solution to $A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ is $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ tells us that 

$$
\textrm{Null}(A)=\{ \mathbf{0} \},
$$

 or alternatively, 

$$
\textrm{dim(Null}(A)) = \textrm{nullity}(A)=0.
$$

- Furthermore, if $\textrm{dim(Null}(A))=0$ then $A$ has no *non-pivot* columns, or equivalently, all the columns of $A$ are *pivot columns*. So 

$$
\textrm{dim(Col}(A))=\textrm{rank}(A)=n.
$$

- Finally, since $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ and its basis has $n$ linearly independent vectors, we can conclude that 

$$
\textrm{Col}(A)=\mathbb{R}^n.
$$

All the results mentioned above can be summarized in the following theorem, called the **invertible matrix theorem**:

*Let $A$ be an $n \!\times\! n$ matrix. Then we have the following equivalence:*

:step/content.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true, given that $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix and  $det(A)=1?$

Select all that apply.

- **I.** $A$ is not invertible

- **II.** $\text{rank}(A)=4$

- **III.** $A$ has $5$ pivot columns
:step/content.:question/worked-solution:
Since $A$ is a $5\times 5$ matrix, the invertible matrix theorem states the following:

$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\{\,\begin{aligned} & \text{Col}(A)={R}^{5} \\  & \text{dim(Col}(A))=5=\text{rank}(A) \\  & \text{Null}(A)=\{0\} \\  & \text{dim(Null}(A))=0=\text{nullity}(A)\end{aligned}$

With that in mind, let's examine each statement in turn. 

- Statement I is false. Indeed,   a matrix $A$ is invertible if and only if $det(A)\ne 0.$ Since here we have $det(A)=1\ne 0,$ our matrix $A$ must be  invertible.

- Statement II is false. Indeed, by the invertible matrix theorem
$A$ is invertible $\,⇔\,\text{rank}(A)=5.$

- Statement III is true. Since $\text{rank}(A)=5$,  it must be $\text{dim(Col}(A))=5$ which, in turn, means that  $A$ has $5$ pivot columns.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
To find the pivots and pivot columns of a general matrix, we first need to convert the matrix to row echelon form (REF).

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The **pivots** of a matrix in row echelon form are the first non-zero entries in each row of the matrix.

For example, given the matrix 
![](images/ad/addf5cd1e1219a1e1ce28f3d27d1b000b3a99640ff89a62e55b66f3a5cdb3521.svg)
which is in row echelon form, let's find the pivots of $A.$

- The first non-zero entry in the first row is the entry $a_{11}=1.$ So this is a pivot.

- The first non-zero entry of the second row is $a_{22}=1.$ So this is also a pivot.

- The first non-zero entry in the third row is $a_{34}=1.$ Therefore this is a pivot.

The pivots of $A$ are highlighted below.

![](images/96/96dcf8cf9f0d387e0539ea04dd7ae4a498534361ad6bd5ed3bb119ae21f0416a.svg)

The **pivot columns** of a matrix in row echelon form are simply the columns in which the pivots appear.

For our matrix $A$, we can see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $4$th columns.

The non-pivot columns are the columns that do not contain a pivot. So for the matrix $A,$ the only non-pivot column is the $3$rd column.

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Non-Pivot Columns of a Matrix in Row Echelon Form

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
To find the pivots and pivot columns of a general matrix, we first need to convert the matrix to row echelon form (REF).

- The pivots of any matrix are the pivots of its row equivalent REF matrix.

- The pivot columns of a matrix are the pivot columns of its row equivalent REF matrix.

To reduce a general $n\times m$ matrix to row echelon form, we follow a similar procedure to the $2\times 2$ and $3\times 3$ cases, as we'll see in the next example.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The **pivots** of a matrix in row echelon form are the first non-zero entries in each row of the matrix.

For example, given the matrix 
![](images/ad/addf5cd1e1219a1e1ce28f3d27d1b000b3a99640ff89a62e55b66f3a5cdb3521.svg)
which is in row echelon form, let's find the pivots of $A.$

- The first non-zero entry in the first row is the entry $a_{11}=1.$ So this is a pivot.

- The first non-zero entry of the second row is $a_{22}=1.$ So this is also a pivot.

- The first non-zero entry in the third row is $a_{34}=1.$ Therefore this is a pivot.

The pivots of $A$ are highlighted below.

![](images/96/96dcf8cf9f0d387e0539ea04dd7ae4a498534361ad6bd5ed3bb119ae21f0416a.svg)

The **pivot columns** of a matrix in row echelon form are simply the columns in which the pivots appear.

For our matrix $A$, we can see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $4$th columns.

The non-pivot columns are the columns that do not contain a pivot. So for the matrix $A,$ the only non-pivot column is the $3$rd column.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
To find the pivots and pivot columns of a general matrix, we first need to convert the matrix to row echelon form (REF).

- The pivots of any matrix are the pivots of its row equivalent REF matrix.

- The pivot columns of a matrix are the pivot columns of its row equivalent REF matrix.

To reduce a general $n\times m$ matrix to row echelon form, we follow a similar procedure to the $2\times 2$ and $3\times 3$ cases, as we'll see in the next example.

A square matrix $A$ is **symmetric** if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A^T = A
$$

Equivalently, an $n\times n$ matrix is symmetric if $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $1 \leq i,j\leq n.$

If $A$ is symmetric, this really means that it is symmetric across its main diagonal. 

For example, the matrix 

![](images/0f/0f62a89f8da1ab7bfb86d46fddb441e95e5e3a9554e5a88662691b4df40e19af.svg)

is symmetric since $A^T = A.$ 

On the other hand, the matrix 

![](images/78/780de3c3f66b1037e4152224f4aa98b65b8b1b859adfe7c3881bb830d7eecd66.svg)

is not symmetric. Indeed, since $b_{12} \neq b_{21},$ we have $B^T \neq B.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Identifying Symmetric Matrices

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose that $A$ is a symmetric matrix. Then, we have the following properties:

- $-A$ is symmetric

- $A^m$ is symmetric for any positive integer $m$

- $A^{-1}$ is symmetric for nonsingular $A$

If $A$ and $B$ are $n\times n$ symmetric matrices, we have the following properties:

- $A+B$ is symmetric

- The product $A\cdot B$ is *not* always symmetric. For example, if 
![](images/e4/e41d28b6c6562ada530024fe6ab29cc16447dce14b2f741b8b35758618c78103.svg)
then the product $A\cdot B$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cdot B & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\,\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

 
which is *not* symmetric.

Finally, the following two properties can be used to construct symmetric matrices:

- $A + A^T$ is symmetric for any *square* matrix $A$

- $A^T A$ and $A A^T$ are symmetric for *any* matrix $A$

The last property is true for *any* $m\times n$ matrix. This property is particularly useful, as we'll discover in future lessons.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. If $A$ is *any* $n\times n$ matrix, then $A+A^T$ is always symmetric.

II. The difference between two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is symmetric.

III. The product of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is symmetric.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A = A^T
$$

Equivalently, $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+{A}^{T})^{T} & ={A}^{T}+({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}+A \\  & =A+{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the sum or difference between two symmetric matrices is symmetric.

- Statement III is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 
![](images/81/812e9888b920e0338fd72116464b8b96c8c272f95f180cd46aa3f1db9afac8d2.svg)
Their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrix 

$\,$ $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

However, ${A}^{3}$ is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{3} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}+{B}^{T} \\  & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A-B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}-{B}^{T} \\  & =A-B.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
To take the **transpose of a matrix**, we interchange each of its columns with the corresponding row. That is, row $1$ becomes column $1,$ row $2$ becomes column $2,$ and so on. A superscript ${}^{T}$ is used to denote the transpose operation.

For example, the transpose of the $2 \times 3$ matrix ${X}$ is the following $3 \times 2$ matrix $X^T\mathbin{:}$

$$
{X} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		{\color{red}7} & {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}-4}  \\
        		{\color{blue}-3} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

        \qquad\implies\qquad

	{X}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		{\color{red}7} & {\color{blue}-3}  \\
        		{\color{red}2} & {\color{blue}1}  \\
        		{\color{red}-4} & {\color{blue}0}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack
$$

The first row of $X$ becomes the first column of $X^T,$ and the second row of $X$ becomes the second column of $X^T.$

Note that transposing a matrix swaps its dimensions. In general, we have the following property:

> *When a matrix is transposed, its dimensions switch from $m \times n$ to $n \times m.$*

Also, notice that the transpose of a column vector is a row vector:

$$
{A} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		5  \\
        		4  \\
                        2 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

       \qquad \implies\qquad

	{A}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		5 & 4 & 2
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack
$$

Similarly, the transpose of a row vector is a column vector:

$$
{B} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		8 & -10 & 0 & 6
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

        \qquad\implies\qquad

	{B}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		8  \\
                        -10  \\
                        0  \\
                        6
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Determining the Dimensions of the Transpose of a Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Remember that transposing a matrix swaps the rows and columns. So, if $B=A^T,$ then $b_{ij}=a_{ji}$ for all values of $i$ and $j.$ 

Geometrically, when a matrix is transposed, the diagonal elements (those with $i=j$) remain the same while all other elements are reflected across the diagonal.  For example,

$$
{A} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7}  \\
        		1 & \color{red}{6}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

      \qquad  \implies\qquad

	{A}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & 1  \\
        		\color{blue}{7} & \color{red}{6} 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack.
$$

Also,  transposing a matrix twice results in the original matrix. More precisely, for any matrix $A,$ we have

$$
\left( A^T\right)^T = A.
$$

This happens because, in the first transpose, we swap the rows of $A$ for the columns, and then in the second transpose, we swap them back again. For example,

$$
{A} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7}  \\
        		1 & \color{red}{6}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

      \quad  \implies\quad

	{A}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & 1  \\
        		\color{blue}{7} & \color{red}{6} 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

      \quad  \implies\quad

	\left( {A}^T\right)^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7}  \\
        		1 & \color{red}{6} 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack =A.
$$

Finally, for any numbers $c_1,c_2$ and any $m \times n$ matrices $A,B$ we have the following rule:

$$
(c_1 A \pm c_2 B)^T = c_1 A^T \pm c_2 B^T
$$

17592186162586.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal. 

With that in mind, let's examine each matrix in turn.

- $P$ is a symmetric matrix. Indeed, $P={P}^{T}.$

- $Q$ is *not* a symmetric matrix. Since ${q}_{13}\ne {q}_{31},$ we obtain $Q\ne {Q}^{T}.$

$$
Q=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 & -1 \\ -2 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 & 9\end{bmatrix}
$$

- $R$ is *not* a symmetric matrix. Since ${r}_{12}\ne {r}_{21},$ we obtain $R\ne {R}^{T}.$

$$
R=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$P$ only."

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose that $A$ is a symmetric matrix. Then, we have the following properties:

- $-A$ is symmetric

- $A^m$ is symmetric for any positive integer $m$

- $A^{-1}$ is symmetric for nonsingular $A$

If $A$ and $B$ are $n\times n$ symmetric matrices, we have the following properties:

- $A+B$ is symmetric

- The product $A\cdot B$ is *not* always symmetric. For example, if 
![](images/e4/e41d28b6c6562ada530024fe6ab29cc16447dce14b2f741b8b35758618c78103.svg)
then the product $A\cdot B$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}A\cdot B & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}\,\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

 
which is *not* symmetric.

Finally, the following two properties can be used to construct symmetric matrices:

- $A + A^T$ is symmetric for any *square* matrix $A$

- $A^T A$ and $A A^T$ are symmetric for *any* matrix $A$

The last property is true for *any* $m\times n$ matrix. This property is particularly useful, as we'll discover in future lessons.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

I. If $A$ is *any* $n\times n$ matrix, then $A+A^T$ is always symmetric.

II. The difference between two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is symmetric.

III. The product of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is symmetric.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A = A^T
$$

Equivalently, $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+{A}^{T})^{T} & ={A}^{T}+({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}+A \\  & =A+{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the sum or difference between two symmetric matrices is symmetric.

- Statement III is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 
![](images/81/812e9888b920e0338fd72116464b8b96c8c272f95f180cd46aa3f1db9afac8d2.svg)
Their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

\begin{aligned}(A+{A}^{T})^{T} & ={A}^{T}+({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}+A \\  & =A+{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the sum or difference between two symmetric matrices is symmetric.

- Statement III is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 
![](images/81/812e9888b920e0338fd72116464b8b96c8c272f95f180cd46aa3f1db9afac8d2.svg)
Their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Powers of matrices are similar to powers of numbers. If $A$ is a matrix, then $A^n$ is $A$ multiplied by itself $n$ times: 

$$
A^n = \underbrace{A\:\cdot\: A\:\cdot\: \ldots \:\cdot\: A}_{\Large{n\text{ times}}}
$$

For $A$ to be conformable with itself, $A$ needs to be a square matrix. So we can only take powers of square matrices.

To demonstrate, suppose that
![](images/81/81537bed0eafc982114b89fc84baeac44f7a75997c89df5a0f89b8b0a00b2da3.svg)

Then we can calculate $A^2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot 2 & 3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1 \\ 2\cdot 3+1\cdot 2 & 2\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 8 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

We say that $A^0 = I,$ the identity matrix of the same dimension as $A.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding a Power of a Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Now that we know how to compute powers of matrices, we can evaluate polynomials where the input is a square matrix. 

For example, consider the polynomial

$$
f(X) = X^2 + 4X + 3.
$$

Note that, in order to evaluate this polynomial for an input matrix $X,$ we need to interpret any constants as multiples of the identity matrix. So, we interpret the polynomial as

$$
f(X) = X^2 + 4X + 3I.
$$

For example, if ![](images/6a/6abb7cbdef9c5d7b23d8519468b174de369cfe4af4b9f8c4578ce7dc74812f63.svg) then

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and we can evaluate $f(A)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{2}+4A+3I \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}+4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4 & 4 \\ 0 & 8\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+4+3 & 3+4+0 \\ 0+0+0 & 4+8+3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 7 \\ 0 & 15\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

So, we want to find $f(D)=-D^2+3D+2I.$

Let's calculate $D^2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{D}^{2} & =D\cdot D \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -10 \\ 0 & 9\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(D) & =-{D}^{2}+3D+2I \\  & =-\begin{bmatrix}1 & -10 \\ 0 & 9\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 0 & -3\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 10 \\ 0 & -9\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 & 15 \\ 0 & -9\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1+3+2 & 10+15+0 \\ 0 & -9-9+2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 25 \\ 0 & -16\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

17592186162676.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.

- **I.** If $A$ is *any* matrix, then $A{A}^{T}$ is always symmetric.
- **II.** The sum of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
- **III.** The product of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
17592186162676.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any $m\times n$ matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A{A}^{T})^{T} & =({A}^{T})^{T}{A}^{T} \\  & =A{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}+{B}^{T} \\  & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 

$\,$ $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\,$ and $\,B=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}.$ 

However, their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

17592186162694.:question/problem:
Which of the following statements are true?
- **I.** If $A$ is *any*  $n\times n$  matrix, then $A-{A}^{T}$ is always symmetric.
- **II.** The sum of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
- **III.** If $A$ is symmetric, then ${A}^{-1}$ is always symmetric (if it exists).

Select all that apply.
17592186162694.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrix 

$\,$ $A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

However, $A-{A}^{T}$ is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}A-{A}^{T} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 0\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, for any two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)^{T} & ={A}^{T}+{B}^{T} \\  & =A+B.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any non-singular symmetric matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}({A}^{-1})^{T} & =({A}^{T})^{-1} \\  & ={A}^{-1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II and III only."

- **II.** If $A$ is *any* $n\times n$ matrix, then $A+{A}^{2}$ is always symmetric.
- **III.** If $A$ is *any*  $n\times n$ matrix, then $A{A}^{T}-{A}^{T}A$ is always symmetric.
17592186275136.:question/worked-solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any diagonal matrices $A$ and $B,$ their product $AB$ is also diagonal, and any diagonal matrix is symmetric.

- Statement II is false. As a counterexample, consider the matrix 

$\,$ $A=\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$

However, $A+{A}^{2}$ is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}A+{A}^{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -1 \\ 1 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement III is true. Indeed, for any square matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A{A}^{T}-{A}^{T}A)^{T} & =(A{A}^{T})^{T}-({A}^{T}A)^{T} \\  & =({A}^{T})^{T}{A}^{T}-{A}^{T}({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & =A{A}^{T}-{A}^{T}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

The dimension of the column space of a matrix $A$ is called the **rank of $A$**. It's usually denoted by $\textrm{rank}(A)$. So, 

$$
\textrm{rank}(A) = \textrm{dim}(\textrm{Col}(A)).
$$

For example, to find the rank of 
![](images/b9/b91bd53b8f1807be516e2477b37fbcd9c3a7415d6cf848d84aa085bc510b5eb4.svg)
we write $A$ in row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that there are $2$ pivot columns, namely, the $1$st and the $2$nd. This implies that the first and the second columns of $A$ form a basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)$ and, therefore, the dimension of $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is equal to $2.$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We know that $\textrm{rank}(A)$ is the number of pivot columns in $A$. 

Since $A$ has $7$ columns and $3$ of them are non-pivots, then the number of pivot columns in $A$ is 

$$
7-3=4.
$$

Therefore, $\textrm{rank}(A)=4$.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Note that the number of pivot columns always coincides with the number of non-zero rows in the corresponding row echelon form matrix.
So, technically, 

$\textrm{rank}(A)$ is the number of *pivot columns* in the corresponding row echelon form matrix of $A$.

Or, equivalently,

$\textrm{rank}(A)$ is the number of *non-zero rows* in the corresponding row echelon form matrix of $A$.

The dimension of the column space of a matrix $A$ is called the **rank of $A$**. It's usually denoted by $\textrm{rank}(A)$. So, 

$$
\textrm{rank}(A) = \textrm{dim}(\textrm{Col}(A)).
$$

For example, to find the rank of 
![](images/b9/b91bd53b8f1807be516e2477b37fbcd9c3a7415d6cf848d84aa085bc510b5eb4.svg)
we write $A$ in row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 6 & 4 & 10\end{bmatrix} & {R}_{3} & :={R}_{3}+(-2){R}_{1} \\  & ∼\begin{bmatrix}3 & 2 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

From the reduced matrix above, we see that there are $2$ pivot columns, namely, the $1$st and the $2$nd. This implies that the first and the second columns of $A$ form a basis of $\textrm{Col}(A)$ and, therefore, the dimension of $\textrm{Col}(A)$ is equal to $2.$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Note that the number of pivot columns always coincides with the number of non-zero rows in the corresponding row echelon form matrix.
So, technically, 

$\textrm{rank}(A)$ is the number of *pivot columns* in the corresponding row echelon form matrix of $A$.

Or, equivalently,

$\textrm{rank}(A)$ is the number of *non-zero rows* in the corresponding row echelon form matrix of $A$.

Note that the number of pivot columns always coincides with the number of non-zero rows in the corresponding row echelon form matrix.
So, technically, 

$\textrm{rank}(A)$ is the number of *pivot columns* in the corresponding row echelon form matrix of $A$.

Or, equivalently,

$\textrm{rank}(A)$ is the number of *non-zero rows* in the corresponding row echelon form matrix of $A$.

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+B)C & =AC+BC, \\ C(A+B) & =CA+CB.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$
AB+AC=A(B+C).
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}B+C & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 0 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & -3 & 5\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 & -3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 \\ -4 & 3 & -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & ={I}_{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}AB+AC & =A(B+C) \\  & =A{I}_{3} \\  & =A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}4 & 3 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -2 \\ -1 & 2 & 5\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$
AC+BC=(A+B)C.

$$

$$

 

Finally, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}AC+BC & =(A+B)C \\  & =4{I}_{3}C \\  & =4C \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8\sqrt{5} & -4 & 12 \\ 0 & 4\sqrt{3} & 16 \\ -8 & 12 & 20\text{ }\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

$$

$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating a Matrix Product Using the Distributive Law

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
If $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are three matrices that are conformable for multiplication, then they follow the **associative law**:

$$
\left( AB\right) C = A\left( BC\right)
$$

So, when we wish to compute a product $ABC,$ we don't always have to start by multiplying $AB.$ Alternatively, we can start by multiplying $BC,$ and then multiply $A$ by the result. 

Sometimes rearranging the parentheses might make the computations slightly easier.
:step/content.:tutorial/title: The Associative Law for Matrix Multiplication

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:

$$
ABC = (AB)C = A(BC).
$$

Notice that $A$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix, $B$ is a $3 \times 3$ matrix, and $C$ is a $3 \times 1$ matrix. Therefore, 

- multiplying $A$ by $B$, we will obtain a $3 \times 3$ matrix that will require finding $9$ entries, while

- multiplying $B$ by $C$, we will obtain a $3 \times 1$ matrix that will require finding only $3$ entries.

So, we find the product $BC$ first:

$$
\begin{aligned}BC & =\begin{bmatrix}-2 & 5 & -4 \\ 2 & 1 & 1 \\ -4 & 3 & -1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-2 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 0 \\ 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply $A$ by $BC\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}ABC & =A(BC) \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & 0 \\ 4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 0 \\ 8\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ -4 \\ 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}

III. $A(B+C) = AB+AC$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's consider the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. Matrix multiplication is associative, so $(AB)C = A(BC)$ in general.

- Statement II is false. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $A(B+C) = AB + AC$ in general. However, since matrix multiplication is not commutative, we have

$$
AB + AC  \neq BA + CA.
$$

- Statement III is true. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $(A+B)C = AC+BC,$ and $A(B+C) = AB+AC$ in general.

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.

If $A,$ $B,$ and $C$ are three matrices that are conformable for multiplication, then they follow the **associative law**:

$$
\left( AB\right) C = A\left( BC\right)
$$

So, when we wish to compute a product $ABC,$ we don't always have to start by multiplying $AB.$ Alternatively, we can start by multiplying $BC,$ and then multiply $A$ by the result. 

Sometimes rearranging the parentheses might make the computations slightly easier.

In general, matrix multiplication is **not** commutative. In other words, given two general matrices $A$ and $B$ that are conformable for multiplication, we have

$$
AB \neq BA.
$$

However, some particular matrices may satisfy this property. For instance, $AI = IA$ (where $I$ is the identity matrix).

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Given that $A, B,$ and $C$ are $6 \times 6$ matrices, which of the following statements are always true?

I. $A(BC) = (AB)C$

II. $A(B+C) = BA+CA$

III. $A(B+C) = AB+AC$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's consider the statements one by one.

- Statement I is true. Matrix multiplication is associative, so $(AB)C = A(BC)$ in general.

- Statement II is false. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $A(B+C) = AB + AC$ in general. However, since matrix multiplication is not commutative, we have

$$
AB + AC  \neq BA + CA.
$$

- Statement III is true. Matrix multiplication is distributive, so $(A+B)C = AC+BC,$ and $A(B+C) = AB+AC$ in general.

Therefore, only statements I and III are true.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we want to solve the following system of linear equations using the elimination method:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y &=1 \\ x-y &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

As it stands, adding the two equations will not eliminate any of the variables. 

However, suppose we want to eliminate the variable $x$. We begin by multiplying the second equation by $\color{blue}-1$, which gives the following equivalent system:

![](images/72/724119f2404af61332fcabbb5cda3522f9d338a4c6427084e5901e1ca7cd4498.svg)

Then, we add the two resulting equations together. This will eliminate the variable $x,$ allowing us to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\cancel{x}+2y & =1 \\ -\cancel{x}+y & =2 \\ (2y+y) & =(1+2) \\ 3y & =3 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\{ x+12y=-35; \left(-7x+2y=-13\right)\cdot (-6)
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}

42x-12y&=78 \\

x&=1
\end{aligned}
$$

Suppose we want to solve the following system of linear equations using the elimination method:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y &=1 \\ x-y &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

As it stands, adding the two equations will not eliminate any of the variables. 

However, suppose we want to eliminate the variable $x$. We begin by multiplying the second equation by $\color{blue}-1$, which gives the following equivalent system:

![](images/72/724119f2404af61332fcabbb5cda3522f9d338a4c6427084e5901e1ca7cd4498.svg)

Then, we add the two resulting equations together. This will eliminate the variable $x,$ allowing us to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\cancel{x}+2y & =1 \\ -\cancel{x}+y & =2 \\ (2y+y) & =(1+2) \\ 3y & =3 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $y=1.$ However, we still need to find $x.$ To do this, we substitute $y=1$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x-y & =-2 \\ x-(1) & =-2 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-1$ and $y=1,$ which can be expressed as $(-1, 1).$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose we want to solve the following system of linear equations using the elimination method:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x+2y &=1 \\ x-y &=-2\end{aligned}\right.
$$

As it stands, adding the two equations will not eliminate any of the variables. 

However, suppose we want to eliminate the variable $x$. We begin by multiplying the second equation by $\color{blue}-1$, which gives the following equivalent system:

![](images/72/724119f2404af61332fcabbb5cda3522f9d338a4c6427084e5901e1ca7cd4498.svg)

Then, we add the two resulting equations together. This will eliminate the variable $x,$ allowing us to solve for $y\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\cancel{x}+2y & =1 \\ -\cancel{x}+y & =2 \\ (2y+y) & =(1+2) \\ 3y & =3 \\ y & =1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the solution must have $y=1.$ However, we still need to find $x.$ To do this, we substitute $y=1$ back into one of the equations. Let's choose the second equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}x-y & =-2 \\ x-(1) & =-2 \\ x & =-1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the system of equations is $x=-1$ and $y=1,$ which can be expressed as $(-1, 1).$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The systems of equations we've encountered up to now have all had *exactly one solution*.

For example, consider the following system:

$$
{y = 2x + 1; y = 1 - x
$$

Using either substitution or elimination, we can show that the solution $(x,y)$ to this system is $(0,1)$. This is the *only* solution, and it tells us the point of intersection between the two corresponding lines.

![](images/bd/bd7edb530e16b853318a3e38785c7b6353c1b54f10ee3c4e2de7da915450f6d9.png)

In general, systems of equations can have

- *exactly one* solution (like the example above)
- *infinitely many* solutions
- *no solutions*

To determine the number of solutions to a system of equations, we solve it using either substitution or elimination and interpret the result.

Let's look at a system of equations with infinitely many solutions.

Consider the following system of equations:

$$
{3x - y =-2; 6x - 2y =-4
$$

To show that this system has infinitely many solutions, we solve the system using elimination.

Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $-2$, then we get a $-6x$ term that can cancel with the $6x$ term in the second equation:

$$
{3x - y =-2 \mid \mid \cdot (-2); 6x - 2y =-4
$$

When we add the two equations, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-6x + 2y &= 4 \\
6x - 2y &= -4 \\
0 &= (4 - 4) \\
0 &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The statement $0=0$ is *always* true. This implies that this system of equations has *infinitely many solutions*.

Geometrically, this means that the equations

$$
{\color{red}3x - y =-2}
$$

and

$$
{\color{blue}6x -2y=-4}
$$

both represent the *same straight line*. In other words, the two lines **coincide**.

![](images/e9/e9e98008aa5972889efdd3af0689da310c69bca06dd410a391a37e22aa8b0098.png)

These two lines intersect at an infinite number of points. The system has infinitely many solutions because there are infinitely many intersection points.

Another way to see that this system has infinitely many solutions is to notice that the lines are nonzero multiples of each other.

For example, if we multiply the equation of the first line by $2$, we get the second line!

$$
3x - y =-2; 2 \cdot (3x - y) = 2 \cdot (-2); 6x - 2y =-4
$$

Let's now look at an example of a system with *no solutions*.
:step/content.:tutorial/title: A System With Infinitely Many Solutions

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Show that the following system of equations has no solution.

${4x + 2y = 4; 2x + y = 4$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's start by solving the system using elimination.

Notice that if we multiply the second equation by $-2$, then we will get a $-4x$ term that can cancel with the $4x$ term in the first equation:

$$
{4x + 2y = 4; 2x + y = 4 \mid \mid \cdot (-2)
$$

When we add the two equations, it turns out that both variables cancel, and we obtain a false statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
4x + 2y &= 4 \\
- 4x - 2y &= -8 \\
0 &= (4 - 8) \\
0 &= -4
\end{aligned}
$$

The statement $0=-4$ is *always false*. Therefore, we conclude that the system has *no solutions*.

Geometrically, this means that the corresponding lines *do not intersect*. In other words, they are *parallel.*

As we've seen, the solutions of a linear system

$$
{a_{1}x + b_{1}y = c_{1}; a_{2}x + b_{2}y = c_{2}
$$

correspond to the points of intersection of the two lines. There are three possibilities:

| ![](images/a1/a1e58afecd7b919f6fd77b48f7bcb7219e54d2f86f8ef07df619505a4643bdd4.png) | ![](images/a4/a466524eb95d85e6c383a37955fffbf02fc9391b0b09a85fce7f44ab934bdc91.png) | ![](images/c7/c73a9f1bfbdd4efa1826b77a7bce1a9e1cbb13e61d718ffe18404e13a31a34f4.png) |
| --- | ---: | ---: |

- Case $(a)$ shows two parallel lines. Because there are no points of intersection, the system has *no solutions*. This happens whenever the lines have the *same* slope but *different* $y$-intercepts.
- Case $(b)$ shows two lines intersecting at a single point. Because there is a single point of intersection, the system has *one solution*.
- Case $(c)$ shows two lines that coincide. Because there are infinitely many points of intersection, the system has *infinitely many* solutions. This happens whenever the lines have the *same* slope and *same* $y$-intercept. In such cases, the two lines are nonzero multiples of each other.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: At how many points do the lines $x - 2y = 2$ and $10y - 5x = -10$ intersect?

The number of points of intersection between the two lines is equal to the number of solutions of the corresponding system:

$$
{x - 2y = 2; 10y - 5x =-10
$$

We will solve the system using substitution. First, we solve for $x$ in the first equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
x - 2y &= 2 \\
x &= 2y + 2
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute

$$
x=2y+2
$$

into the second equation and solve for $y$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
10y - 5x &= -10 \\
10y - 5(2y + 2) &= -10 \\
10y - 10y - 10 &= -10 \\
- 10 &= -10
\end{aligned}
$$

The result is a statement that's always true. Therefore, we conclude that the system has infinitely many solutions.

Consequently, the lines intersect at infinitely many points (i.e., they coincide).

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding the Number of Intersection Points of Two Lines

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
When a system of equations has one solution, we can describe the solution as a single point $(x,y)$. This represents the point where the two lines intersect.

Now, suppose a system of equations has *infinitely many* solutions. Can we describe the solutions to the system in a similar way?

Indeed, we can. To demonstrate, consider the following system:

$$
{3x - y =-2; 6x - 2y =-4
$$

Earlier, we showed that this system has infinitely many solutions. Therefore, the corresponding lines coincide.

Our goal is to express *all* the solutions of this system in the form $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$. To do this, we find the corresponding $y$-coordinate for each $x$-coordinate by solving one of the equations for $y$. It doesn't matter which, so let's pick the first equation.

$$
3x - y =-2⇒y = 3x + 2
$$

Therefore, for any given $x$-value, the corresponding $y$-value is

$$
y = 3x+2
$$

Finally, we can express the intersection points as

$$
({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}}) = \left({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{3x+2}}\right)
$$

where $\color{blue}x$ is *any* number.
:step/content.:tutorial/title: Describing General Solutions of Systems With Infinitely Many Solutions

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Let's go back to our system of equations:

$$
{3x - y =-2; 6x - 2y =-4
$$

We showed that the set of intersection points $(x,y)$ is given by

$$
(x,y) = \left(x,3x + 2\right)
$$

When we add the two equations, it turns out that both variables cancel, and we obtain a true statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
14x + 10y &= 8 \\
-14x - 10y &= -8 \\
0 &= (8 - 8) \\
0 &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a true statement, we conclude that there are infinitely many solutions to the system. Therefore, the lines have infinitely many intersection points.

We want to find an expression that represents every solution to the system. Any value of $x$ can be chosen, and we can find the corresponding $y$-coordinate for each $x$-coordinate by solving one of the lines for $y$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
7x + 5y &= 4 \\
5y &= 4 - 7x \\
y &= \frac{4 - 7x}{5} \\
y &= \frac{4}{5} - \frac{7}{5}x
\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x$ be the free coordinate.

Therefore, the points of intersection are

$$
\left(u,\frac{4}{5} - \frac{7}{5}u \right)
$$

where $u$ is any number.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Consider the following system of equations:

$$
{3x - y =-2; 6x - 2y =-4
$$

To show that this system has infinitely many solutions, we solve the system using elimination.

Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $-2$, then we get a $-6x$ term that can cancel with the $6x$ term in the second equation:

$$
{3x - y =-2 \mid \mid \cdot (-2); 6x - 2y =-4
$$

When we add the two equations, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-6x + 2y &= 4 \\
6x - 2y &= -4 \\
0 &= (4 - 4) \\
0 &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

The statement $0=0$ is *always* true. This implies that this system of equations has *infinitely many solutions*.

Geometrically, this means that the equations

$$
{\color{red}3x - y =-2}
$$

and

$$
{\color{blue}6x -2y=-4}
$$

both represent the *same straight line*. In other words, the two lines **coincide**.

![](images/e9/e9e98008aa5972889efdd3af0689da310c69bca06dd410a391a37e22aa8b0098.png)

These two lines intersect at an infinite number of points. The system has infinitely many solutions because there are infinitely many intersection points.

Another way to see that this system has infinitely many solutions is to notice that the lines are nonzero multiples of each other.

For example, if we multiply the equation of the first line by $2$, we get the second line!

$$
3x - y =-2; 2 \cdot (3x - y) = 2 \cdot (-2); 6x - 2y =-4
$$

Let's now look at an example of a system with *no solutions*.

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
When a system of equations has one solution, we can describe the solution as a single point $(x,y)$. This represents the point where the two lines intersect.

Now, suppose a system of equations has *infinitely many* solutions. Can we describe the solutions to the system in a similar way?

Indeed, we can. To demonstrate, consider the following system:

$$
{3x - y =-2; 6x - 2y =-4
$$

Earlier, we showed that this system has infinitely many solutions. Therefore, the corresponding lines coincide.

Our goal is to express *all* the solutions of this system in the form $({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}})$. To do this, we find the corresponding $y$-coordinate for each $x$-coordinate by solving one of the equations for $y$. It doesn't matter which, so let's pick the first equation.

$$
3x - y =-2⇒y = 3x + 2
$$

Therefore, for any given $x$-value, the corresponding $y$-value is

$$
y = 3x+2
$$

Finally, we can express the intersection points as

$$
({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{y}}) = \left({\color{blue}{x}},{\color{red}{3x+2}}\right)
$$

where $\color{blue}x$ is *any* number.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find all points of intersection of the lines $3x+2y=2$ and $6x+4y=4$.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The points of intersection of the lines correspond to the solutions of the following system:

$$
{3x + 2y = 2; 6x + 4y = 4
$$

We will solve the system using elimination. Notice that if we multiply the first equation by $-2$, then we will get a $-6x$ term that can cancel with the $6x$ term in the second equation:

$$
{3x + 2y = 2 \mid \mid \cdot (-2); 6x + 4y = 4
$$

When we add the two equations, it turns out that both variables cancel, and we obtain a true statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}
-6x - 4y &= -4 \\
6x + 4y &= 4 \\
0 &= (-4 + 4) \\
0 &= 0
\end{aligned}
$$

Because we obtained a true statement, we conclude that there are infinitely many solutions to the system. Therefore, the lines have infinitely many intersection points.

We want to find an expression that represents every solution to the system. Any value of $x$ is a solution, and we can find the corresponding $y$-coordinate for each $x$-coordinate by solving one of the lines for $y$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
3x + 2y &= 2 \\
2y &= 2 - 3x \\
y &= \frac{2 - 3x}{2} \\
y &= 1 - \frac{3}{2}x
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the points of intersection are

$$
\left(x,1-\dfrac{3}{2}x \right)
$$

where $x$ is any number.

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Multiplying Two Matrices When They Are Conformable

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
It's possible to express matrix multiplication using index notation.

To see how, first let $C=AB,$ where $A$ and $B$ are two matrices that are conformable for multiplication.

Then $c_{\color{red}{i}\color{blue}{j}}$ represents the entry at the intersection of the $\color{red}i$th row and $\color{blue}j$th column in $C.$

To compute $c_{\color{red}{i}\color{blue}{j}},$ we take the dot product of the $\color{red}i$th row of $\color{red}A$ and the $\color{blue}j$th column of ${\color{blue}B},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{i1} & {a}_{i2} & ⋯ & {a}_{in}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Here, the first factor is a $3 \times 1$ matrix and the second factor is a $1 \times 2$ matrix. 

There is $1$ column in the first matrix and $1$ row in the second matrix, so the product is well defined:

$$
\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} \times {\color{green}\fbox{1}} {\color{green}\checkmark} {\color{green}\fbox{1}} \times \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2} = 
	\bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{3} \times \bbox[lightgray, 2pt]{2}
$$

Computing the product, we have

$$
\eqalign {
    \left\lbrack
    \begin{matrix}
       -1  \\
 	0  \\
        -2
    \end{matrix}
    \right\rbrack

    \left\lbrack
    \begin{matrix}
        2 & -5
    \end{matrix}
    \right\rbrack

	&= 

    \left\lbrack
    \begin{matrix}
        (-1)\cdot 2 & (-1)\cdot (-5)  \\
        0\cdot 2 & 0\cdot (-5) \\
        (-2)\cdot 2 & (-2)\cdot (-5)
    \end{matrix}
    \right\rbrack \[5pt]

	&=

    \left\lbrack
    \begin{matrix}
       -2 & 5  \\
       0 &  0  \\
       -4 &  10 
    \end{matrix}
    \right\rbrack 
}
$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Here, $A$ is a $2\times 1$ matrix and $B$ is a $1\times 2$ matrix. 

There is $1$ column in $A$ and $1$ row in $B,$ so $A$ and $B$ are conformable for multiplication: 

$$
{A}_{2\times \boxed{\text{1}}}{\cdot }_{✓}{B}_{\boxed{\text{1}}\times 2}={AB}_{2\times 2}
$$

Let's compute $AB,$ one element at a time:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & ∗ \\ ∗ & ∗\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,-3=-1\cdot 3 \\  & \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ ∗ & ∗\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,1=(-1)\cdot (-1) \\  & \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ -9 & ∗\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,-9=(-3)\cdot 3 \\  & \begin{bmatrix}-1 \\ -3\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ -9 & 3\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,3=(-3)\cdot (-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 
$AB=\begin{bmatrix}-3 & 1 \\ -9 & 3\end{bmatrix}.$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find $ST$,  if  $S=\begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}$ and $T=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 6 & 4\end{bmatrix}.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Here, $S$ is a $1\times 4$ matrix and $T$ is a $4\times 2$ matrix. 

There are $4$ columns in $S$ and $4$ rows in $T,$ so $S$ and $T$ are conformable for multiplication:

$$
{S}_{1\times \boxed{\text{4}}}{\cdot }_{✓}{T}_{\boxed{\text{4}}\times 2}={ST}_{1\times 2}
$$

Let's compute $ST,$ one element at a time:

$$
\begin{aligned} & \begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 6 & 4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}24 & ∗\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,24=2\cdot 1+(-3)\cdot 0+1\cdot (-2)+4\cdot 6 \\  & \begin{bmatrix}2 & -3 & 1 & 4\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -2 \\ 0 & 4 \\ -2 & 1 \\ 6 & 4\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}24 & 1\end{bmatrix}, &  & \,1=2\cdot (-2)+(-3)\cdot 4+1\cdot 1+4\cdot 4\end{aligned}

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Powers of matrices are similar to powers of numbers. If $A$ is a matrix, then $A^n$ is $A$ multiplied by itself $n$ times: 

$$
A^n = \underbrace{A\:\cdot\: A\:\cdot\: \ldots \:\cdot\: A}_{\Large{n\text{ times}}}
$$

For $A$ to be conformable with itself, $A$ needs to be a square matrix. So we can only take powers of square matrices.

To demonstrate, suppose that
![](images/81/81537bed0eafc982114b89fc84baeac44f7a75997c89df5a0f89b8b0a00b2da3.svg)

Then we can calculate $A^2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot 2 & 3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1 \\ 2\cdot 3+1\cdot 2 & 2\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 8 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

We say that $A^0 = I,$ the identity matrix of the same dimension as $A.$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Finding a Power of a Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Now that we know how to compute powers of matrices, we can evaluate polynomials where the input is a square matrix. 

For example, consider the polynomial

$$
f(X) = X^2 + 4X + 3.
$$

Note that, in order to evaluate this polynomial for an input matrix $X,$ we need to interpret any constants as multiples of the identity matrix. So, we interpret the polynomial as

$$
f(X) = X^2 + 4X + 3I.
$$

For example, if ![](images/6a/6abb7cbdef9c5d7b23d8519468b174de369cfe4af4b9f8c4578ce7dc74812f63.svg) then

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and we can evaluate $f(A)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{2}+4A+3I \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}+4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4 & 4 \\ 0 & 8\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+4+3 & 3+4+0 \\ 0+0+0 & 4+8+3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 7 \\ 0 & 15\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Now, we can evaluate $f(C):$

$$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Consider the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{bmatrix}.$  Find $f(A)$ if $f(X)={X}^{2}+X-1.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we rewrite the polynomial, interpreting any constants as multiples of the identity matrix:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(X) & ={X}^{2}+X-1 \\  & ={X}^{2}+X-I\end{aligned}
$$

So, we want to find $f(A)={A}^{2}+A-I.$

Let's calculate ${A}^{2}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we can evaluate $f(A):$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{2}+A-I \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+3-1 & 0-2+0 \\ 0+4+0 & 1-3-1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 4 & -3\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Powers of matrices are similar to powers of numbers. If $A$ is a matrix, then $A^n$ is $A$ multiplied by itself $n$ times: 

$$
A^n = \underbrace{A\:\cdot\: A\:\cdot\: \ldots \:\cdot\: A}_{\Large{n\text{ times}}}
$$

For $A$ to be conformable with itself, $A$ needs to be a square matrix. So we can only take powers of square matrices.

To demonstrate, suppose that
![](images/81/81537bed0eafc982114b89fc84baeac44f7a75997c89df5a0f89b8b0a00b2da3.svg)

Then we can calculate $A^2$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =A\cdot A \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}\cdot \begin{bmatrix}3 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 3+(-1)\cdot 2 & 3\cdot (-1)+(-1)\cdot 1 \\ 2\cdot 3+1\cdot 2 & 2\cdot (-1)+1\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}7 & -4 \\ 8 & -1\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

We say that $A^0 = I,$ the identity matrix of the same dimension as $A.$

Now that we know how to compute powers of matrices, we can evaluate polynomials where the input is a square matrix. 

For example, consider the polynomial

$$
f(X) = X^2 + 4X + 3.
$$

Note that, in order to evaluate this polynomial for an input matrix $X,$ we need to interpret any constants as multiples of the identity matrix. So, we interpret the polynomial as

$$
f(X) = X^2 + 4X + 3I.
$$

For example, if ![](images/6a/6abb7cbdef9c5d7b23d8519468b174de369cfe4af4b9f8c4578ce7dc74812f63.svg) then

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{2} & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix},\end{aligned}
$$

and we can evaluate $f(A)$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(A) & ={A}^{2}+4A+3I \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}+4\begin{bmatrix}1 & 1 \\ 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}+3\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}4 & 4 \\ 0 & 8\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}1+4+3 & 3+4+0 \\ 0+0+0 & 4+8+3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}8 & 7 \\ 0 & 15\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$
