:step/content.:tutorial/content:
To take the **transpose of a matrix**, we interchange each of its columns with the corresponding row. That is, row $1$ becomes column $1,$ row $2$ becomes column $2,$ and so on. A superscript ${}^{T}$ is used to denote the transpose operation.

For example, the transpose of the $2 \times 3$ matrix ${X}$ is the following $3 \times 2$ matrix $X^T\mathbin{:}$

$$
{X} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		{\color{red}7} & {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}-4}  \\
        		{\color{blue}-3} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

        \qquad\implies\qquad

	{X}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		{\color{red}7} & {\color{blue}-3}  \\
        		{\color{red}2} & {\color{blue}1}  \\
        		{\color{red}-4} & {\color{blue}0}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack
$$

The first row of $X$ becomes the first column of $X^T,$ and the second row of $X$ becomes the second column of $X^T.$

Note that transposing a matrix swaps its dimensions. In general, we have the following property:

> *When a matrix is transposed, its dimensions switch from $m \times n$ to $n \times m.$*

Also, notice that the transpose of a column vector is a row vector:

$$
{A} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		5  \\
        		4  \\
                        2 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

       \qquad \implies\qquad

	{A}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		5 & 4 & 2
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack
$$

Similarly, the transpose of a row vector is a column vector:

$$
{B} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		8 & -10 & 0 & 6
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

        \qquad\implies\qquad

	{B}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		8  \\
                        -10  \\
                        0  \\
                        6
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Determining the Dimensions of the Transpose of a Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Remember that transposing a matrix swaps the rows and columns. So, if $B=A^T,$ then $b_{ij}=a_{ji}$ for all values of $i$ and $j.$ 

Geometrically, when a matrix is transposed, the diagonal elements (those with $i=j$) remain the same while all other elements are reflected across the diagonal.  For example,

$$
{A} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7}  \\
        		1 & \color{red}{6}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

      \qquad  \implies\qquad

	{A}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & 1  \\
        		\color{blue}{7} & \color{red}{6} 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack.
$$

Also,  transposing a matrix twice results in the original matrix. More precisely, for any matrix $A,$ we have

$$
\left( A^T\right)^T = A.
$$

This happens because, in the first transpose, we swap the rows of $A$ for the columns, and then in the second transpose, we swap them back again. For example,

$$
{A} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7}  \\
        		1 & \color{red}{6}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

      \quad  \implies\quad

	{A}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & 1  \\
        		\color{blue}{7} & \color{red}{6} 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

      \quad  \implies\quad

	\left( {A}^T\right)^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7}  \\
        		1 & \color{red}{6} 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack =A.
$$

Finally, for any numbers $c_1,c_2$ and any $m \times n$ matrices $A,B$ we have the following rule:

$$
(c_1 A \pm c_2 B)^T = c_1 A^T \pm c_2 B^T
$$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: Properties of the Transpose of a Matrix

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
To take the **transpose of a matrix**, we interchange each of its columns with the corresponding row. That is, row $1$ becomes column $1,$ row $2$ becomes column $2,$ and so on. A superscript ${}^{T}$ is used to denote the transpose operation.

For example, the transpose of the $2 \times 3$ matrix ${X}$ is the following $3 \times 2$ matrix $X^T\mathbin{:}$

$$
{X} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		{\color{red}7} & {\color{red}2} & {\color{red}-4}  \\
        		{\color{blue}-3} & {\color{blue}1} & {\color{blue}0}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

        \qquad\implies\qquad

	{X}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		{\color{red}7} & {\color{blue}-3}  \\
        		{\color{red}2} & {\color{blue}1}  \\
        		{\color{red}-4} & {\color{blue}0}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack
$$

The first row of $X$ becomes the first column of $X^T,$ and the second row of $X$ becomes the second column of $X^T.$

Note that transposing a matrix swaps its dimensions. In general, we have the following property:

> *When a matrix is transposed, its dimensions switch from $m \times n$ to $n \times m.$*

Also, notice that the transpose of a column vector is a row vector:

$$
{A} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		5  \\
        		4  \\
                        2 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

       \qquad \implies\qquad

	{A}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		5 & 4 & 2
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack
$$

Similarly, the transpose of a row vector is a column vector:

$$
{B} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		8 & -10 & 0 & 6
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

        \qquad\implies\qquad

	{B}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		8  \\
                        -10  \\
                        0  \\
                        6
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Remember that transposing a matrix swaps the rows and columns. So, if $B=A^T,$ then $b_{ij}=a_{ji}$ for all values of $i$ and $j.$ 

Geometrically, when a matrix is transposed, the diagonal elements (those with $i=j$) remain the same while all other elements are reflected across the diagonal.  For example,

$$
{A} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7}  \\
        		1 & \color{red}{6}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

      \qquad  \implies\qquad

	{A}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & 1  \\
        		\color{blue}{7} & \color{red}{6} 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack.
$$

Also,  transposing a matrix twice results in the original matrix. More precisely, for any matrix $A,$ we have

$$
\left( A^T\right)^T = A.
$$

This happens because, in the first transpose, we swap the rows of $A$ for the columns, and then in the second transpose, we swap them back again. For example,

$$
{A} = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7}  \\
        		1 & \color{red}{6}
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

      \quad  \implies\quad

	{A}^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & 1  \\
        		\color{blue}{7} & \color{red}{6} 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack

      \quad  \implies\quad

	\left( {A}^T\right)^T = 
    		\left\lbrack
    		\begin{matrix}
        		\color{red}{3} & \color{blue}{7}  \\
        		1 & \color{red}{6} 
    		\end{matrix}
    		\right\rbrack =A.
$$

Finally, for any numbers $c_1,c_2$ and any $m \times n$ matrices $A,B$ we have the following rule:

$$
(c_1 A \pm c_2 B)^T = c_1 A^T \pm c_2 B^T
$$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We can use matrices to solve systems of linear equations. To do this, we need to set up the **augmented matrix** for the system.

As an example, let's consider the system of equations below.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{\color{red}2}x+{\color{red}5}y &={\color{blue}-1} \\ {\color{red}-3}x+{\color{red}7}y &={\color{blue}1}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

First, we find the **coefficient matrix**, which consists of the coefficients of the variables:

$$
\begin{matrix}{\color{red}2} & {\color{red}5} \\ {\color{red}-3} & {\color{red}7}\end{matrix}
$$

Then, we create the **augmented matrix**. This is the coefficient matrix augmented with the column that represents the right-hand sides of the equations:

$$
\begin{array}{cc|c}{\color{red}2} & {\color{red}5} & {\color{blue}-1} \\ {\color{red}-3} & {\color{red}7} & {\color{blue}1}\end{array}
$$

In the future, we will learn how to use coefficient and augmented matrices to solve systems of equations. But for now, let's practice setting them up.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
What is the coefficient matrix for the following system of linear equations?

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=1 \\ 2y &=-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
First, we organize the system so that every variable has a coefficient:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}x-2y &=1 \\ 0x+2y &=-1\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The coefficient matrix consists of the coefficients of the variables:

$$
\left\lbrack
	\begin{matrix}
		1 & -2  \\
		0 & 2 
	\end{matrix}
	\right\rbrack
$$

We can use matrices to solve systems of linear equations. To do this, we need to set up the **augmented matrix** for the system.

As an example, let's consider the system of equations below.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{\color{red}2}x+{\color{red}5}y &={\color{blue}-1} \\ {\color{red}-3}x+{\color{red}7}y &={\color{blue}1}\end{aligned}\right.
$$

First, we find the **coefficient matrix**, which consists of the coefficients of the variables:

$$
\begin{matrix}{\color{red}2} & {\color{red}5} \\ {\color{red}-3} & {\color{red}7}\end{matrix}
$$

Then, we create the **augmented matrix**. This is the coefficient matrix augmented with the column that represents the right-hand sides of the equations:

$$
\begin{array}{cc|c}{\color{red}2} & {\color{red}5} & {\color{blue}-1} \\ {\color{red}-3} & {\color{red}7} & {\color{blue}1}\end{array}
$$

In the future, we will learn how to use coefficient and augmented matrices to solve systems of equations. But for now, let's practice setting them up.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}7x+9y-z &=14 \\ 11-10x &=-18y \\ -y+12x &=9z\end{aligned}\right.
$$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First, we organize the system so that the variables are ordered $x,y,z$ on the left-hand side, the constants are on the right-hand side, and every variable has a coefficient:

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}7x+9y-z &=14 \\ -10x+18y+0z &=-11 \\ 12x-y-9z &=0\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The coefficient matrix consists of the coefficients of the variables:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}7 & 9 & -1 \\ -10 & 18 & 0 \\ 12 & -1 & -9\end{bmatrix}
$$

The augmented matrix  is the coefficient matrix augmented with the column that represents the right-hand sides of the equations:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}7 & 9 & -1 & 14 \\ -10 & 18 & 0 & -11 \\ 12 & -1 & -9 & 0\end{array}\right]
$$

Identify the points that lie on the line $y=5-2x.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The plotted points correspond to the $xy$-pairs $A(0,5), B(2,1)$ and $C(3,0).$ 

To check whether a point lies on the line, we substitute the coordinates of the point into the equation and determine whether the resulting statement is true.

- Substituting the point $A(0,5)$ results in a true statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5-2x \\ (5) & =5-2(0) \\ 5 & =5\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $A$ does lie on the line:

- Substituting the point $B(2,1)$ results in a true statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5-2x \\ (1) & =5-2(2) \\ 1 & =1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the point $B$ does lie on the line:

- Substituting the point $C(3,0)$ results in a false statement:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =5-2x \\ (0) & =5-2(3) \\ 0 & =-1\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, only points $A$ and $B$ lie on the line.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Sketch the graph of $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We need to find two distinct points that lie on our line. Any two points will do!

It is often easiest to pick one of the points to have an $x$-coordinate of $x=0.$ So, for the first point, we will let the $x$-coordinate be $x=0.$ Then the $y$-coordinate is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(0)+3 \\  & =0+3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first point is $(0,3).$

For the second point, let's choose $x=4.$ Then the $y$-coordinate is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(4)+3 \\  & =-2+3 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second point is $(4,1).$

Finally, we plot those two points on the $xy$-plane and draw a line through them. This is the graph of $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.$

![](images/36/36689081acaacb24a09826c3927388697e77d92caeca900d053d33d0f99d2b8c.png)

$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Sketch the graph of $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We need to find two distinct points that lie on our line. Any two points will do!

It is often easiest to pick one of the points to have an $x$-coordinate of $x=0.$ So, for the first point, we will let the $x$-coordinate be $x=0.$ Then the $y$-coordinate is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(0)+3 \\  & =0+3 \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the first point is $(0,3).$

For the second point, let's choose $x=4.$ Then the $y$-coordinate is

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-\frac{1}{2}x+3 \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}(4)+3 \\  & =-2+3 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the second point is $(4,1).$

Finally, we plot those two points on the $xy$-plane and draw a line through them. This is the graph of $y=-\dfrac{1}{2}x+3.$

![](images/36/36689081acaacb24a09826c3927388697e77d92caeca900d053d33d0f99d2b8c.png)

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Which of the following gives the graph of the straight line below?

I. $y=2x-1$

II. $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x-1$

III. $2x-y=1$

![](images/93/93dc9d447c15e4597549996b1f0b533cf86783b5cc5df032a4c46d4ca8934abc.png)
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Let's pick two distinct points on the line. For example, we can choose $A$ and $B$ with coordinates $(0,-1)$ and $(2,3)$, respectively.

![](images/a9/a9f18453dedb1763908825301f80ef86307d3a3aceaf678bbe8579a42a0996f5.png)

Now, we substitute the coordinates of both points in our equations. If both points satisfy an equation, then we can conclude that the equation represents the line in the graph. Otherwise, if any point does *not* satisfy the equation, then we can conclude that the equation does *not* represent the line in the graph.

- Equation I: $y=2x-1.$
Substituting the coordinates of $A(0,-1)$ and $B(2,3),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1) & =2(0)-1 \\ -1 & =-1\,✓ \\ (3) & =2(2)-1 \\ 3 & =3\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $y=2x-1$ is an equation of the line in the graph.

- Equation II: $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x-1.$
Substituting the coordinates of $A(0,-1)$ and $B(2,3),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}(-1) & =\frac{1}{2}(0)-1 \\ -1 & =-1\,✓ \\ (3) & =\frac{1}{2}(2)-1 \\ 3 & =0\,\times \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $y=\dfrac{1}{2}x-1$ is *not* an equation of the line in the graph.

- Equation III: $2x-y=1.$
Substituting the coordinates of $A(0,-1)$ and $B(2,3),$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}2(0)-(-1) & =1 \\ 1 & =1\,✓ \\ 2(2)-(3) & =1 \\ 1 & =1\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $2x-y=1$ is an equation of the line in the graph.

Of the given equations, the only equations that represented the line in the graph were $y=2x-1$ and $2x-y=1,$ corresponding to answer choices I and III. Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Multiplying a Matrix With Variable Entries by a Column Vector

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
An alternative, yet equivalent, procedure for multiplying a matrix by a column vector involves adding scaled columns of the matrix $A$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =\begin{bmatrix}a & c \\ b & d\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3 \\ 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =3\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}+2\begin{bmatrix}c \\ d\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3a \\ 3b\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}2c \\ 2d\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}3a+2c \\ 3b+2d\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

If we denote 
$\begin{bmatrix}a \\ b\end{bmatrix}$
and 
$\begin{bmatrix}c \\ d\end{bmatrix}$ 
then we can also write the multiplication as follows:

$$
A\mathbf{x}={\color{blue}3}\mathbf{u}_1 + {\color{blue}2} \mathbf{u}_2
$$

The expression above is a **linear combination** of the vectors $\mathbf{u}_1$ and $\mathbf{u}_2,$ where the corresponding coefficients are given by the entries of the vector $\mathbf{x}.$

17592186101054.:activity/title: Multiplying a Matrix by a Column Vector

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
To multiply a matrix by a column vector, we multiply each row in the matrix by the column vector using the dot product.

For example, suppose we would like to multiply 
$\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 6 & 7\end{bmatrix}$
and 
$\begin{bmatrix}-3 \\ 4\end{bmatrix}$

First, we write the multiplication as follows:

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 6 & 7\end{bmatrix}
$$

The result of the multiplication is another column vector $\mathbf{y}$ with the same dimensions as $\mathbf{x}$.
Now, we calculate the entries of the product (shown as $\ast$'s in the equation above).

To find $y_1,$ the $1$st component of $\mathbf{y}$, we calculate the dot product of the $1$st row of $A$ and the vector $\mathbf{x}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 6 & 7\end{bmatrix}
$$

To find $y_2,$ the $2$nd component of $\mathbf{y},$ we calculate the dot product of the $2$nd row of $A$ and the vector $\mathbf{x}\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 6 & 7\end{bmatrix}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{bmatrix}9 \\ 10\end{bmatrix}
$$

$Z=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 \\ 2 & -7\end{bmatrix}$
and
$x=\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix}.$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We multiply each row in the matrix by the column vector using the dot product. Multiplying the first row, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 \\ 2 & -7\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}1\cdot 1+(-4)\cdot (-1) \\ ∗\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ ∗\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying the second row, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{bmatrix}1 & -4 \\ 2 & -7\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 2\cdot 1+(-7)\cdot (-1)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 
$Zx=\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ 9\end{bmatrix}.$

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We can multiply matrices by numbers. This type of multiplication is known as **scalar multiplication**. Here, a **scalar** is just a number.

For example, consider the matrix

$$
{A}=
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To multiply ${A}$ by the scalar $2,$ we just multiply each entry of ${A}$ by $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2A & =2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 3 \\ 2\cdot 2 & 2\cdot 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In general, to multiply a $m \times n$ matrix $A$ by a scalar $c,$ we multiply each entry of $A$ by $c$ as follows:

$$
cA 
	=
	c \cdot
	\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} & … & {a}_{1n} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22} & … & {a}_{2n} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ {a}_{m1} & {a}_{m2} & … & {a}_{mn}\end{bmatrix} 
	= 
	\begin{bmatrix}c{a}_{11} & c{a}_{12} & … & c{a}_{1n} \\ c{a}_{21} & c{a}_{22} & … & c{a}_{2n} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ c{a}_{m1} & c{a}_{m2} & … & c{a}_{mn}\end{bmatrix}
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
If 

$$
k {A} =
\begin{bmatrix}
        	1 & 3 & 4  \\
        	6 & 0 & -2
    	\end{bmatrix},
$$

where 

$$
{A} =
\begin{bmatrix}
        	2 & 6 & 8  \\
        	12 & 0 & -4
    	\end{bmatrix}
$$

and $k$ is a scalar, calculate the value of $k.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To express $kA,$ we multiply each entry of $A$ by $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}kA & =k\cdot \begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 & 8 \\ 12 & 0 & -4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2k & 6k & 8k \\ 12k & 0 & -4k\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we set the above result equal to the matrix given for $kA$ in the problem statement:

$$
\left\lbrack
    	\begin{matrix}
        	2k & 6k & 8k  \\
        	12k & 0 & -4k
    	\end{matrix}
    	\right\rbrack
=
\left\lbrack
    	\begin{matrix}
        	1 & 3 & 4  \\
        	6 & 0 & -2
    	\end{matrix}
    	\right\rbrack
$$

We can solve for $k$ by equating any two corresponding (nonzero) elements. Let's choose the top-left elements, $2k$ and $1.$ Equating these elements, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}2k & =1 \\ k & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** We would still get the same result if we chose any other two corresponding (nonzero) elements.

$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating a Linear Combination of Two Matrices

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Since scalar multiplication is done entry-wise, it obeys the same kind of rules as multiplication of real numbers.

For example, for any numbers $c_1, c_2$ and any matrix $A,$ we can perform scalar multiplication in any order: 

$$
c_1 (c_2 A) = (c_1 c_2) A = c_2 (c_1 A)
$$

Moreover, we can distribute a matrix over the sum or difference of scalars:

$$
(c_1 \pm c_2)A = c_1A \pm c_2A
$$

We can also distribute scalar multiplication over the sum or difference of two matrices:

$$
c (A \pm B) = c A \pm c B
$$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: Properties of Scalar Multiplication of Matrices

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
We can multiply matrices by numbers. This type of multiplication is known as **scalar multiplication**. Here, a **scalar** is just a number.

For example, consider the matrix

$$
{A}=
\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}.
$$

To multiply ${A}$ by the scalar $2,$ we just multiply each entry of ${A}$ by $2\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2A & =2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 3 \\ 2\cdot 2 & 2\cdot 4\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 6 \\ 4 & 8\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

In general, to multiply a $m \times n$ matrix $A$ by a scalar $c,$ we multiply each entry of $A$ by $c$ as follows:

$$
cA 
	=
	c \cdot
	\begin{bmatrix}{a}_{11} & {a}_{12} & … & {a}_{1n} \\ {a}_{21} & {a}_{22} & … & {a}_{2n} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ {a}_{m1} & {a}_{m2} & … & {a}_{mn}\end{bmatrix} 
	= 
	\begin{bmatrix}c{a}_{11} & c{a}_{12} & … & c{a}_{1n} \\ c{a}_{21} & c{a}_{22} & … & c{a}_{2n} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ c{a}_{m1} & c{a}_{m2} & … & c{a}_{mn}\end{bmatrix}
$$

$W=\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -3 \\ -5 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We multiply each entry of $W$ by $0,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}0W & =0\begin{bmatrix}1 & -1 & -3 \\ -5 & 0 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0\cdot 1 & 0\cdot (-1) & 0\cdot (-3) \\ 0\cdot (-5) & 0\cdot 0 & 0\cdot 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}0 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

    	\end{bmatrix}

$$

$$

    	\begin{matrix}

=

        	6 & 0 & -2
    	\end{matrix}
    	\right\rbrack
$$

We can solve for $k$ by equating any two corresponding (nonzero) elements. Let's choose the top-left elements, $2k$ and $1.$ Equating these elements, we get

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Since scalar multiplication is done entry-wise, it obeys the same kind of rules as multiplication of real numbers.

For example, for any numbers $c_1, c_2$ and any matrix $A,$ we can perform scalar multiplication in any order: 

$$
c_1 (c_2 A) = (c_1 c_2) A = c_2 (c_1 A)
$$

Moreover, we can distribute a matrix over the sum or difference of scalars:

$$
(c_1 \pm c_2)A = c_1A \pm c_2A
$$

We can also distribute scalar multiplication over the sum or difference of two matrices:

$$
c (A \pm B) = c A \pm c B
$$

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem:
Calculate $2A+\frac{1}{2}B$, where
$A=\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
$B=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2\end{bmatrix}$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
We multiply each entry of $A$ by $2$ and each entry of $B$ by $\dfrac{1}{2},$ and then add the resulting matrices, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2A+\frac{1}{2}B & =2\begin{bmatrix}1 & 5 \\ 1 & 2\end{bmatrix}+\frac{1}{2}\begin{bmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 4 & 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 5 \\ 2\cdot 1 & 2\cdot 2\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}\cdot 0 & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2 \\ \frac{1}{2}\cdot 4 & \frac{1}{2}\cdot 2\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 10 \\ 2 & 4\end{bmatrix}+\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2+0 & 10+1 \\ 2+2 & 4+1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 11 \\ 4 & 5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate $2H-3L$, where
$H=\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}$
and
$L=\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix}$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
We multiply each entry of $H$ by $2$ and each entry of $L$ by $3,$ and then subtract the resulting matrices, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2H-3L & =2\begin{bmatrix}3 & -2 \\ 2 & -1\end{bmatrix}-3\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2\cdot 3 & 2\cdot (-2) \\ 2\cdot 2 & 2\cdot (-1)\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}3\cdot 0 & 3\cdot 1 \\ 3\cdot 2 & 3\cdot 1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -4 \\ 4 & -2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}0 & 3 \\ 6 & 3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6-0 & -4-3 \\ 4-6 & -2-3\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}6 & -7 \\ -2 & -5\end{bmatrix}\end{aligned}
$$

17592186060927.:tutorial/content:
Since scalar multiplication is done entry-wise, it obeys the same kind of rules as multiplication of real numbers.

For example, for any numbers $c_1, c_2$ and any matrix $A,$ we can perform scalar multiplication in any order: 

$$
c_1 (c_2 A) = (c_1 c_2) A = c_2 (c_1 A)
$$

Moreover, we can distribute a matrix over the sum or difference of scalars:

$$
(c_1 \pm c_2)A = c_1A \pm c_2A
$$

We can also distribute scalar multiplication over the sum or difference of two matrices:

$$
c (A \pm B) = c A \pm c B
$$
